passages.title: Instruments That Argue
text: It is customary to treat scientific instruments as neutral windows: the telescope merely extends the eye, the thermometer merely registers what was already there. On this picture, theory lives in the minds of scientists and in the pages of journals, while instruments are passive servants whose only virtue is accuracy. I want to suggest that this picture has the relationship backward. Instruments are not servants of theory so much as condensed arguments, and a great deal of what a scientific community believes is stored in its equipment rather than in its explicit doctrines.

Consider the early thermometer. Before anyone could measure temperature, someone had to decide that the expansion of a liquid in a sealed tube tracked something real and uniform, and that equal increments of expansion corresponded to equal increments of heat. These were not observations; they were commitments, and contested ones. Different liquids expanded at different rates, and for decades makers disagreed about which substance told the truth. When mercury eventually won, it won partly because it was convenient to work with, not because anyone had proven its fidelity. Yet once mercury thermometers filled laboratories, the assumptions built into them became invisible. A student reading a scale was, without knowing it, endorsing a theory of heat she could not have stated.

This is why I find it misleading to say that experiments test theories while instruments merely collect data. Every reading is already shaped by choices about what counts as a signal and what counts as noise, and those choices were made by craftsmen and committees long before the experiment began. When a new result conflicts with an established one, scientists rarely blame the instrument first, not because instruments are infallible but because doubting them would mean reopening settled arguments that no one remembers having.

None of this implies that science is arbitrary. Embedded assumptions can be dug out and examined, and the history of science contains many episodes in which a discrepancy finally forced someone to ask what an instrument had been taking for granted. My claim is more modest: the rationality of science is partly a rationality of things. To understand why a field believes what it does, we should read its catalogs of apparatus as carefully as we read its theories.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the main idea of the passage?
o: Instruments are neutral windows that extend human perception.
Not quite. This is the neutral-window picture that paragraph 1 says has the relationship backward.
Instruments embody theoretical commitments that often go unexamined.
Correct: Paragraph 1 calls instruments condensed arguments, and paragraphs 2 and 3 show their assumptions going unexamined.
Scientific conclusions are arbitrary because instruments are biased.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says none of this implies that science is arbitrary.
Mercury thermometers were less accurate than earlier designs.
Not quite. The passage never says mercury was less accurate. It says its fidelity was not proven.
qs.x: Correct: A main-idea question asks for the author's thesis, and this author states it early. Paragraph 1 says the picture of instruments as neutral windows 'has the relationship backward,' that 'Instruments are not servants of theory so much as condensed arguments,' and that much of what a community believes 'is stored in its equipment rather than in its explicit doctrines.' Paragraphs 2 and 3 show how built-in assumptions become invisible, and paragraph 4 says they can still be examined. So the main idea is that instruments embody theoretical commitments that often go unexamined. Why the others are wrong: instruments as neutral windows is the view the author argues against; saying conclusions are arbitrary because instruments are biased overshoots, since paragraph 4 says 'None of this implies that science is arbitrary'; saying mercury thermometers were less accurate than earlier designs is never claimed, because mercury won partly for convenience, not because it was proven worse. Trap: Picking the view the author sets out to overturn.

qs.q: According to the passage, mercury became the standard thermometric liquid partly because it:
o: had been proven to expand uniformly with heat
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says mercury won 'not because anyone had proven its fidelity.'
was cheaper than any competing liquid
Not quite. Cost is never mentioned in the passage.
was endorsed after a decisive experiment
Not quite. The passage describes no decisive experiment. It says convenience helped decide the matter.
was convenient to work with
Correct: Paragraph 2 says mercury won partly because it was convenient to work with.
qs.x: Correct: This is a detail question, so find the sentence about mercury. Paragraph 2 says 'When mercury eventually won, it won partly because it was convenient to work with, not because anyone had proven its fidelity.' So mercury became standard partly because it was convenient to work with. Why the others are wrong: being proven to expand uniformly with heat is the exact opposite of the text, which says no one had proven its fidelity; being cheaper than any competing liquid is never mentioned, so choosing it brings in an assumption the passage doesn't support; being endorsed after a decisive experiment also conflicts with the text, since the point is that the matter was settled without proof. Trap: Choosing the answer that sounds scientific instead of the one the passage states.

qs.q: The author mentions a student reading a thermometer scale primarily to illustrate that:
o: users can unknowingly accept its assumptions
Correct: The student endorses a theory of heat she couldn't state just by reading the scale, so users unknowingly accept built-in assumptions.
students were poorly trained in the theory of heat
Not quite. The point is not poor training. It is that assumptions pass quietly into users.
thermometers were too difficult for beginners to read
Not quite. The passage never says thermometers were hard to read.
early mercury thermometers gave inaccurate readings that misled the scientists who relied on them
Not quite. The author never says the readings were inaccurate, only that commitments are built in.
qs.x: Correct: A 'mentions in order to illustrate' question asks what point the example supports. Paragraph 2 ends: 'A student reading a scale was, without knowing it, endorsing a theory of heat she could not have stated.' The student doesn't know the theory, yet by trusting the scale she accepts it. So the example shows that users can unknowingly accept an instrument's built-in assumptions. Why the others are wrong: saying students were poorly trained in the theory of heat misreads the point, because the passage isn't criticizing training; saying thermometers were too difficult for beginners to read is never claimed, since she reads the scale fine; saying early mercury thermometers gave inaccurate readings is not stated, as the commitments behind the readings are the issue, not their accuracy. Trap: Reading an example about hidden assumptions as a story about errors or poor training.

qs.q: The author would most likely DISAGREE with which statement?
o: Discrepancies sometimes force scientists to examine what instruments assume.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says discrepancies have forced such questions, so the author agrees.
Scientists tend not to blame instruments first when results conflict.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says scientists rarely blame the instrument first, so the author agrees.
Because instruments embed prior choices, scientific results cannot be rationally trusted.
Correct: Paragraph 4 says science is not arbitrary and embedded assumptions can be examined, so the author would reject this.
Catalogs of apparatus deserve study alongside scientific theories.
Not quite. The author recommends reading apparatus catalogs as carefully as theories.
qs.x: Correct: A DISAGREE question means find the statement that goes against the author. Paragraph 4 says 'None of this implies that science is arbitrary. Embedded assumptions can be dug out and examined,' and that science has 'a rationality of things.' So the author would reject the claim that embedded choices mean results cannot be rationally trusted. Why the others are wrong: discrepancies sometimes forcing scientists to examine what instruments assume is in paragraph 4 ('a discrepancy finally forced someone to ask what an instrument had been taking for granted'); scientists tending not to blame instruments first is in paragraph 3; catalogs of apparatus deserving study alongside theories is the author's final recommendation in paragraph 4. The author agrees with all three. Trap: Missing the word DISAGREE and picking a statement the author states.

qs.q: Which historical finding would most strengthen the author's argument?
o: Two rival thermometer designs gave identical readings under every condition tested.
Not quite. Identical readings from rival designs show nothing about hidden assumptions.
Scientists facing a surprising result usually suspected their instruments first and rebuilt them before rechecking the theory.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says scientists rarely blame the instrument first, so this goes against the author.
A measurement dispute ended when one lab's apparatus was adopted, though the question was never resolved.
Correct: A dispute closed by adopting one apparatus, with the question left open, shows equipment settling what argument didn't.
Textbooks of the period stated every assumption built into common instruments, so none went unexamined.
Not quite. If every assumption were stated and examined, the author's claim about invisibility would be weakened.
qs.x: Correct: A 'strengthen' question asks for evidence that fits the author's argument. The author argues in paragraphs 2 and 3 that choices built into equipment can settle questions that were never settled by argument, and then those choices go unexamined, 'reopening settled arguments that no one remembers having.' A dispute that ended because one lab's apparatus was adopted, though the question was never resolved, is exactly that pattern. Why the others are wrong: two rival designs giving identical readings under every condition shows no hidden difference between designs, so it doesn't bear on embedded assumptions; scientists usually suspecting their instruments first goes against paragraph 3, which says they rarely do; textbooks stating every built-in assumption so none went unexamined also contradicts the author's claim that such assumptions become invisible. Trap: Choosing evidence that fits the topic but cuts against the author.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's view of instruments?
o: A test whose rubric quietly encodes one view of intelligence
Correct: Like the thermometer, the rubric carries an unstated theory that users accept just by using it.
A road map that has become outdated as new highways were built
Not quite. An outdated map is about being out of date, not about hidden assumptions.
A microscope whose scratched lens blurs every image it produces, so that every observer who uses it notices the flaw
Not quite. A scratched lens is an obvious physical flaw that observers would notice, not a hidden commitment.
A translator who openly adds her own commentary in brackets
Not quite. Open commentary is visible, while the author's point is that assumptions become invisible.
qs.x: Correct: First state the author's view in plain words: a tool can carry an unstated theory, and people accept it just by using the tool. Paragraph 2 shows it with the thermometer: the student endorses a theory of heat without knowing it. A test whose rubric quietly encodes one view of intelligence works the same way, since test takers and graders accept that view just by using the test. Why the others are wrong: a road map that became outdated as new highways were built is about being out of date, not about hidden assumptions; a microscope with a scratched lens blurs every image, which is a physical defect that every observer would notice, not a hidden commitment; a translator openly adding commentary in brackets is the reverse, since her additions are visible, while the author's point is that the assumptions are invisible. Trap: Choosing a case about error or defect instead of a hidden, accepted assumption.

passages.title: Monkeys in the Margins
text: Open almost any illuminated psalter from the late thirteenth or fourteenth century and you will find, at the edges of the sacred text, a riot of improbable creatures: rabbits jousting on horseback, monkeys playing bagpipes, knights fleeing from snails, a bishop with the hindquarters of a dog. Modern viewers delight in these marginal images, and modern scholars have often explained them as a kind of licensed rebellion, the place where the restless imagination of the illuminator escaped the solemn control of the Church.

The rebellion thesis is appealing because it flatters our own tastes. We prefer our medieval artists to be secret ironists, winking at us across the centuries. But the evidence fits it poorly. Many of the most extravagant margins appear in books commissioned by wealthy and devout patrons, often for private prayer, and there is little sign that those patrons were scandalized. Some images respond closely to words on the same page, punning on a phrase or illustrating a verse in absurdly literal fashion. A rebellion that the authorities paid for, approved, and kept at their bedsides is a strange sort of rebellion.

A better account begins with how such books were used. Devotional reading was slow, repetitive, and meant to be memorized. Medieval writers on memory advised that vivid, even grotesque, images help fix ideas in the mind, and a reader who returned to the same psalm daily needed something to anchor her place and hold her attention. The margins, on this view, are not an escape from devotion but one of its tools: a set of hooks for wandering minds, a way of making the familiar strange enough to be noticed again.

I do not claim that every marginal image had a pious function, or that illuminators never laughed at their betters. Humor and devotion were not opposites for medieval readers, and a single image could amuse and instruct at once. What I resist is the assumption that the center and the margin of the page stood for opposed worlds. They were made by the same hands, paid for by the same purses, and read by the same eyes.

qs.q: The primary purpose of the passage is to:
o: catalog the most common creatures found in medieval margins
Not quite. The creatures in paragraph 1 are a hook for the argument, not its purpose.
argue that medieval illuminators had no sense of humor
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says humor and devotion were not opposites for medieval readers.
show that the Church tightly censored illuminated psalters
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says devout patrons approved these margins, which is the opposite of tight censorship.
challenge the view that marginal images were rebellious and propose a devotional role
Correct: Paragraph 2 argues against the rebellion thesis and paragraph 3 proposes the margins as tools for devotion.
qs.x: Correct: A primary-purpose question asks what the author is doing across the whole passage. Paragraph 1 describes the odd margin creatures and the usual explanation, 'licensed rebellion.' Paragraph 2 says the rebellion thesis 'fits the evidence poorly.' Paragraph 3 offers 'a better account': margins as tools for devotion, hooks for wandering minds. Paragraph 4 sums up that the center and the margin were not opposed worlds. So the purpose is to challenge the rebellion view and propose a devotional role. Why the others are wrong: cataloging the most common creatures only describes paragraph 1, which is a hook for the argument; saying illuminators had no sense of humor contradicts paragraph 4, which says humor and devotion were not opposites; saying the Church tightly censored psalters is nearly the reverse of paragraph 2, where devout patrons paid for and approved these images. Trap: Choosing a detail from the opening paragraph instead of the argument the whole passage makes.

qs.q: The remark that 'a rebellion that the authorities paid for, approved, and kept at their bedsides is a strange sort of rebellion' serves mainly to:
o: suggest that patrons secretly shared the illuminators' rebellious aims and paid to see them expressed
Not quite. The author never says patrons secretly shared rebellious aims.
highlight a tension between the rebellion thesis and evidence about patronage
Correct: The irony points out the clash between a supposed rebellion and the fact that the authorities paid for and approved it.
prove that marginal images had no meaning beyond decoration
Not quite. Paragraph 3 gives the margins a devotional function, so they are not mere decoration.
concede that the rebellion thesis is mostly correct despite the evidence about who paid for the books
Not quite. The remark argues against the thesis. It isn't a concession.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what job the quoted remark does, so read what surrounds it. Paragraph 2 says many extravagant margins appear in books 'commissioned by wealthy and devout patrons, often for private prayer, and there is little sign that those patrons were scandalized.' Then the author says 'A rebellion that the authorities paid for, approved, and kept at their bedsides is a strange sort of rebellion.' The line is ironic: it points out the clash between calling something a rebellion and the fact that those it supposedly defied paid for it. Why the others are wrong: suggesting patrons secretly shared rebellious aims puts a motive in their heads that the author never proposes; proving that margins had no meaning beyond decoration contradicts paragraph 3, which gives them a function; conceding the rebellion thesis is mostly correct is the opposite of the author's point, since the sentence is part of arguing against it. Trap: Reading irony as agreement.

qs.q: According to the passage, medieval writers on memory recommended:
o: reading a psalm only once to preserve its freshness
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says devotional reading was repetitive, with readers returning to the same psalm daily.
vivid, even grotesque images to fix ideas
Correct: Paragraph 3 says medieval writers on memory advised vivid, even grotesque, images to fix ideas.
removing images from books meant for serious study
Not quite. The advice was to use vivid images, not remove them.
restricting illustrations to scenes from scripture so that readers would not be distracted
Not quite. The passage never mentions limiting illustrations to scripture, and the writers favored grotesque images.
qs.x: Correct: This is a detail question, so the answer must be stated in the text. Paragraph 3 says 'Medieval writers on memory advised that vivid, even grotesque, images help fix ideas in the mind.' Why the others are wrong: reading a psalm only once contradicts the same paragraph, which says devotional reading was 'slow, repetitive' and that a reader 'returned to the same psalm daily'; removing images from books meant for serious study is the opposite of the advice about vivid images; restricting illustrations to scenes from scripture is never mentioned, and the author's whole point is that grotesque margin images were useful. Trap: Choosing an answer that sounds like sensible advice rather than the one the passage states.

qs.q: Which discovery would most weaken the author's argument?
o: Further margins that pun on words written on the same page
Not quite. Punning on the page's words supports the author's point that images respond to the text.
More extravagant margins in books that were made for private prayer than in books made for public worship
Not quite. This fits the idea that the margins were made for private devotion.
Some marginal images that were clearly meant to be funny to readers of the time, such as animals in clerical dress
Not quite. Paragraph 4 already allows that some images were funny.
Records showing devout patrons often demanded that offensive margins be scraped away
Correct: Patrons demanding that offensive margins be scraped away would contradict the claim that they approved and weren't scandalized.
qs.x: Correct: A 'weaken' question starts with the author's argument. Paragraph 2 says the rebellion thesis fits poorly because devout, wealthy patrons commissioned and approved the margins and 'there is little sign that those patrons were scandalized.' To weaken that, show that patrons were scandalized. Records showing devout patrons often demanded that offensive margins be scraped away attack this premise directly. Why the others are wrong: more margins that pun on words on the same page matches paragraph 2's point that some images respond closely to the text, so it supports the author; more extravagant margins in private-prayer books than public-worship books fits the idea that these were made for private devotion; some images clearly meant to be funny don't hurt the argument, because paragraph 4 already says illuminators sometimes laughed. Trap: Choosing evidence that is only loosely related to the argument instead of evidence that attacks its premise.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward scholars who hold the rebellion thesis is best described as:
o: skeptical, seeing modern taste more than evidence
Correct: Paragraph 2 says the thesis flatters modern taste and the evidence fits it poorly.
admiring, since they first noticed the marginal images
Not quite. The author never credits these scholars with a discovery.
contemptuous, dismissing any reading of medieval humor
Not quite. Too extreme. The author calls the thesis appealing and grants in paragraph 4 that illuminators sometimes laughed.
neutral, presenting their view without evaluating it or offering an alternative account
Not quite. The author clearly evaluates the thesis and offers a better account.
qs.x: Correct: An attitude question asks for the author's tone toward a group. Paragraph 2 says 'The rebellion thesis is appealing because it flatters our own tastes. We prefer our medieval artists to be secret ironists, winking at us across the centuries. But the evidence fits it poorly.' That is doubt based on evidence, and the author suggests modern taste is driving the thesis. So the attitude is skeptical, seeing modern taste more than evidence. Why the others are wrong: admiring, since they first noticed the marginal images, is not stated, because the author never credits them with noticing anything; contemptuous, dismissing any reading of medieval humor, is too extreme, since the author calls the thesis appealing and in paragraph 4 grants that illuminators sometimes laughed; neutral, presenting their view without evaluating it, is wrong because the author evaluates it and offers a rival account. Trap: Choosing a tone that is too strong or too mild for what the author actually says.

passages.title: The Grammar of Hearsay
text: In a number of the world's languages, including Turkish, Quechua, and Tuyuca, a speaker cannot simply say that it rained last night. The grammar demands that the sentence also mark how the speaker knows: whether she saw the rain, inferred it from wet streets, or was told about it by someone else. Linguists call this feature evidentiality, and it has attracted a good deal of romantic speculation. Surely, the thinking goes, speakers of such languages must be more scrupulous about truth, more careful to distinguish knowledge from rumor, than those of us who can assert anything without citing our sources.

The speculation is understandable but, I think, mistaken in an instructive way. Obligatory marking does not make speakers more honest; it makes a certain kind of information routine. When every sentence must carry an evidential, choosing one becomes as automatic as choosing a verb tense in English, and automatic choices are not moral achievements. A speaker can mark a claim as directly witnessed while lying about it, just as an English speaker can use the past tense to describe events that never happened. The grammar specifies what must be said, not whether what is said is true.

Nor is it clear that languages without grammatical evidentials leave speakers unable to track sources. English speakers have an abundant toolkit: apparently, I hear that, they say, I saw it with my own eyes. The difference is that in English such expressions are optional, and their presence is therefore noticeable. Paradoxically, this may give them more rhetorical force than their grammatical counterparts. When an English speaker goes out of her way to say she saw something herself, listeners take note precisely because she did not have to.

What evidential systems do reveal is that languages differ in which distinctions they make compulsory, and compulsory distinctions shape what speakers attend to in the moment of speaking. That is an interesting claim about habit and attention. It is not a claim about virtue, and conflating the two tells us more about our wish to find moral lessons in grammar than about grammar itself.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's central claim?
o: Languages with evidentials produce more honest speakers than other languages.
Not quite. This is the romantic speculation the author calls mistaken.
English speakers cannot express how they know what they report.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 lists the many ways English speakers can mark their sources.
Obligatory evidential marking shapes attention but does not make speakers more truthful.
Correct: Paragraph 4 says compulsory distinctions shape attention, and paragraph 2 says they don't make speakers more honest.
Grammar has no effect at all on what speakers notice.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says compulsory distinctions do shape what speakers attend to.
qs.x: Correct: A central-claim question asks for the main thesis, and this author's paragraph 4 puts it plainly. Paragraph 1 sets up the 'romantic speculation' that evidentials make speakers more truthful. Paragraph 2 says 'Obligatory marking does not make speakers more honest; it makes a certain kind of information routine.' Paragraph 4 adds that 'compulsory distinctions shape what speakers attend to in the moment of speaking. That is an interesting claim about habit and attention. It is not a claim about virtue.' So the claim has two parts: evidentials shape attention but do not make speakers more truthful. Why the others are wrong: saying evidential languages produce more honest speakers is the speculation the author rejects; saying English speakers cannot express how they know is false, since paragraph 3 lists English expressions like 'apparently' and 'I hear that'; saying grammar has no effect at all on attention contradicts paragraph 4. Trap: Picking the romantic idea the author sets out to correct.

qs.q: The comparison between evidentials and English verb tense in paragraph 2 is used to show that:
o: evidentials and tense are learned at the same age
Not quite. The passage never discusses when either is learned.
English tense is a hidden form of evidentiality that speakers use without noticing
Not quite. The comparison is about automatic grammatical choices, not about tense secretly being evidentiality.
a grammatical requirement does not guarantee that the content is true
Correct: Past tense can describe events that never happened, so a required form doesn't make the content true.
speakers choose tenses more carefully than evidentials, since tense errors are noticed more readily
Not quite. The passage never says tense choices are more careful. It says automatic choices aren't achievements.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what point the tense comparison makes. Paragraph 2 says 'A speaker can mark a claim as directly witnessed while lying about it, just as an English speaker can use the past tense to describe events that never happened. The grammar specifies what must be said, not whether what is said is true.' So the comparison shows that a grammatical requirement doesn't guarantee the content is true. Why the others are wrong: saying evidentials and tense are learned at the same age brings in acquisition, which is never discussed; saying English tense is a hidden form of evidentiality turns the comparison into an identity, but the author only says that both are automatic choices; saying speakers choose tenses more carefully because tense errors are noticed more readily is not stated, and the author actually says automatic choices are not achievements. Trap: Turning an analogy into a claim of sameness.

qs.q: According to the passage, optional source expressions in English may:
o: carry extra rhetorical force because speakers did not have to use them
Correct: Paragraph 3 says they get noticed because speakers did not have to use them, giving more rhetorical force.
be ignored by listeners because they are so common
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says they are noticed, not ignored.
be grammatically required in formal speech
Not quite. The passage calls them optional, not required.
convey less information than grammatical evidentials, because listeners treat them as mere style
Not quite. The passage suggests they may carry more rhetorical force, not less.
qs.x: Correct: This is a detail question. Paragraph 3 says that in English such expressions 'are optional, and their presence is therefore noticeable. Paradoxically, this may give them more rhetorical force than their grammatical counterparts. When an English speaker goes out of her way to say she saw something herself, listeners take note precisely because she did not have to.' Why the others are wrong: being ignored because they are so common contradicts the passage, which says they are noticed because they are optional; being grammatically required in formal speech is false, since the passage calls them optional; conveying less information than grammatical evidentials because listeners treat them as mere style is the reverse of the passage's suggestion of more force. Trap: Choosing a plausible claim that the passage actually contradicts.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would expect a Quechua speaker who wanted to deceive a listener to:
o: be prevented by the grammar from stating the falsehood
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says grammar specifies what must be said, not whether it is true.
be forced to use a hearsay marker for any false claim
Not quite. Nothing forces a hearsay marker onto false claims. The marker states the claimed source.
be detected automatically by native listeners
Not quite. The passage never says listeners can automatically detect lies.
be able to mark a false claim as directly witnessed
Correct: Paragraph 2 says a speaker can mark a claim as witnessed while lying about it.
qs.x: Correct: This asks you to apply the passage to a new case. Paragraph 2 says 'A speaker can mark a claim as directly witnessed while lying about it' because 'The grammar specifies what must be said, not whether what is said is true.' So a Quechua speaker who wanted to deceive could mark a false claim as directly witnessed. Why the others are wrong: being prevented by the grammar from stating a falsehood contradicts the passage, since grammar doesn't check truth; being forced to use a hearsay marker for any false claim isn't a rule anywhere, because the marker reflects the claimed source, not whether the claim is true; being detected automatically by native listeners is never suggested, and the author says the marking doesn't make speakers more honest or listeners more able to detect lies. Trap: Believing that a required marker verifies the claim.

qs.q: Which finding would most challenge the author's position?
o: Children acquire evidential markers later than basic verb tenses.
Not quite. Age of acquisition has no bearing on whether evidentials make speakers honest.
In deception tasks, speakers of evidential languages lie far less often than matched speakers of other languages.
Correct: If evidential speakers lie far less than matched speakers, that supports the link between evidentials and honesty that the author rejects.
English speakers use expressions like 'apparently' very frequently.
Not quite. Frequent English source expressions fit paragraph 3 and don't test the honesty claim.
Speakers of evidential languages sometimes lie using the witness marker, especially when talking with strangers.
Not quite. Lying with the witness marker is exactly what paragraph 2 says can happen, so it supports the author.
qs.x: Correct: A 'challenge the position' question starts with what the author denies. Paragraphs 2 and 4 deny that evidential grammar makes speakers more honest: 'It is not a claim about virtue.' A finding that speakers of evidential languages lie far less often than matched speakers of other languages would support the link the author rejects. Why the others are wrong: children acquiring evidentials later than tenses is about learning, which has no bearing on honesty; English speakers using 'apparently' frequently fits paragraph 3, where English has its own toolkit; evidential-language speakers sometimes lying with the witness marker is the very case paragraph 2 describes, so it supports the author. Trap: Choosing a finding on the same topic that does not touch the author's actual claim.

qs.q: The claim in paragraph 2 that 'automatic choices are not moral achievements' depends on which assumption?
o: Most speakers of evidential languages are dishonest when they are not required to mark their sources.
Not quite. The author says speakers are not more honest, not that they are dishonest.
Moral credit requires something like deliberate effort rather than habitual compliance.
Correct: The claim only works if moral credit requires something like deliberate effort rather than habit.
English has a complete grammatical evidential system.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says English source expressions are optional, not a grammatical system.
Habitual behaviors cannot affect what speakers attend to, even when the habit is repeated thousands of times daily.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says compulsory distinctions shape what speakers attend to.
qs.x: Correct: An assumption question asks what must be true for the author's reasoning to work. Paragraph 2 says choosing an evidential becomes 'as automatic as choosing a verb tense in English, and automatic choices are not moral achievements.' For that to follow, the author must think moral credit needs something more than habit, such as deliberate effort. Without that assumption, an automatic choice could still earn credit. Why the others are wrong: saying most speakers of evidential languages are dishonest when not required to mark sources isn't assumed, because the author says only that they are not more honest; saying English has a complete grammatical evidential system is wrong, since paragraph 3 says English expressions are optional; saying habitual behaviors cannot affect attention contradicts paragraph 4, which says compulsory distinctions shape attention. Trap: Choosing an assumption that contradicts another part of the passage.

passages.title: In Defense of the Vestibule
text: Modern residential design has been at war with the in-between. Open-plan living erased the hallway, the parlor, and the pantry in the name of light and flow, and the vestibule, that small chamber between the front door and the house proper, has nearly vanished from new construction. Architects who remove it are not careless; they see wasted square footage, a dark box that serves no function except to be passed through. In a market that prices homes by area, a room designed for passing through looks like an indulgence.

But the vestibule's function was never primarily spatial. In colder climates it served as an airlock, keeping winter out of the main rooms, and that practical role is real. Its deeper work, however, was social. A vestibule allowed a household to receive a visitor without fully admitting them, to sign for a parcel, decline a salesman, or greet a neighbor while keeping the life of the house out of view. It staged the passage from public to private as a sequence rather than a single step, and in doing so gave both host and guest a moment to adjust their manners.

When the front door opens directly onto the living room, that sequence collapses. Every arrival becomes an intrusion or a full admission; there is no intermediate state. Residents compensate in other ways, with doorbell cameras, with conversations conducted through a half-opened door, with a reluctance to answer at all. These improvisations suggest that the need the vestibule served did not disappear when the room did. It was merely left to be met badly.

I am not arguing that every house needs a small dark room by its front door, nor that older homes were socially superior. Many were built around rigid hierarchies of class and gender that no one should wish to restore. My point is narrower. Architecture encodes assumptions about how people meet, and when we judge rooms only by how much they hold, we lose sight of what they do. Some of the most useful spaces in a building are the ones in which nothing seems to happen.

qs.q: According to the passage, architects remove vestibules mainly because they regard them as:
o: relics of rigid class and gender hierarchies
Not quite. Class and gender hierarchies are the author's concession in paragraph 4, not the architects' reason.
ineffective at keeping cold air out of the house
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the vestibule's airlock role is real.
unpopular with visitors who dislike waiting
Not quite. Visitors' dislike of waiting is never mentioned.
wasted area whose only function is to be passed through
Correct: Paragraph 1 says architects see wasted square footage, a dark box whose only function is to be passed through.
qs.x: Correct: This is a detail question about the architects' reason. Paragraph 1 says 'Architects who remove it are not careless; they see wasted square footage, a dark box that serves no function except to be passed through.' So the architects regard it as wasted area whose only function is to be passed through. Why the others are wrong: relics of rigid class and gender hierarchies is the author's own concession in paragraph 4 about older homes, not the architects' reason; ineffective at keeping cold air out contradicts paragraph 2, which says the airlock role is real; unpopular with visitors who dislike waiting is never mentioned. Trap: Choosing a point the author makes elsewhere and crediting it to the architects.

qs.q: The author mentions doorbell cameras and conversations through a half-opened door in order to:
o: praise technology for replacing outdated rooms
Not quite. The author calls these improvisations a poor way to meet the need.
show that the social need the vestibule met persists and is met with poor substitutes
Correct: Paragraph 3 says these improvisations show the need did not disappear and is now met badly.
argue that residents have become less friendly toward visitors than they were in earlier generations
Not quite. The passage doesn't say residents have become less friendly. It says they lack a way to manage arrivals.
prove that vestibules improved home security
Not quite. Security is never discussed.
qs.x: Correct: A 'mentions in order to' question asks what the examples prove. Paragraph 3 says that without a vestibule, 'Residents compensate in other ways, with doorbell cameras, with conversations conducted through a half-opened door, with a reluctance to answer at all. These improvisations suggest that the need the vestibule served did not disappear when the room did. It was merely left to be met badly.' So the examples show that the social need persists and is being met with poor substitutes. Why the others are wrong: praising technology for replacing outdated rooms is the opposite, since the author calls these improvisations a bad way to meet the need; arguing that residents are less friendly than before is not claimed, because the passage says people lack a way to handle arrivals, not that they got colder; proving that vestibules improved security is never discussed. Trap: Reading evidence of a problem as praise for the fix.

qs.q: Which function of the vestibule does the author consider most important?
o: Keeping winter air out of the main rooms
Not quite. Paragraph 2 calls this role real but contrasts it with the deeper social work.
Staging the passage from public to private as a social sequence
Correct: Paragraph 2 calls the social staging of the move from public to private its deeper work.
Providing extra storage near the front door
Not quite. The passage never mentions storage.
Increasing a home's market value by area
Not quite. Judging homes by area is the architects' view in paragraph 1, which the author questions.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks which function the author ranks highest, so look for a comparison. Paragraph 2 says the airlock role 'is real. Its deeper work, however, was social.' The word 'deeper' marks the social function as the more important. It 'staged the passage from public to private as a sequence rather than a single step.' Why the others are wrong: keeping winter air out is a real function but the author calls it secondary; extra storage near the front door is never mentioned; increasing market value by area is the architects' way of thinking in paragraph 1, which the author argues against. Trap: Choosing the first function mentioned instead of the one the author calls deeper.

qs.q: The concession at the start of paragraph 4 serves primarily to:
o: admit that the argument of paragraph 3 was mistaken
Not quite. The author doesn't retract paragraph 3 and goes on restating the point.
argue that open-plan homes are socially superior
Not quite. The passage argues open plans lost something, not that they are superior.
recommend a vestibule in every new house
Not quite. The first clause says not every house needs a vestibule.
narrow the claim so it is not read as nostalgia for older social arrangements
Correct: The concession narrows the claim so it isn't read as nostalgia for older, hierarchical arrangements.
qs.x: Correct: A 'serves primarily to' question asks about the job of a concession. Paragraph 4 opens: 'I am not arguing that every house needs a small dark room by its front door, nor that older homes were socially superior. Many were built around rigid hierarchies of class and gender that no one should wish to restore. My point is narrower.' The author is limiting the claim so it won't be read as nostalgia for older social arrangements. Why the others are wrong: admitting that paragraph 3's argument was mistaken is not what happens, since the author goes on defending it in the same paragraph; arguing that open-plan homes are socially superior is the opposite of the passage; recommending a vestibule in every new house is explicitly denied in the first clause. Trap: Reading a narrowing of a claim as a retreat from it.

qs.q: Which design would the author most likely praise?
o: A deep, sheltered entry alcove where residents can talk with callers before inviting them in
Correct: It gives residents an in-between space to receive callers before admitting them, as the vestibule did.
An entry converted into a closet to maximize storage space and leave more room for the living area
Not quite. Judging space by what it holds is what paragraph 4 warns against.
A front door opening straight into the kitchen for efficiency
Not quite. A door opening straight into the house collapses the sequence, as paragraph 3 describes.
A glass-walled facade that makes the interior fully visible so that callers and residents can see each other before speaking
Not quite. Full visibility removes the privacy that the vestibule's in-between state protected.
qs.x: Correct: An application question: state what the author values. Paragraph 2 says a vestibule 'allowed a household to receive a visitor without fully admitting them,' creating a sequence from public to private so host and guest could adjust their manners. A deep, sheltered entry alcove where residents can talk with callers before inviting them in gives that in-between state. Why the others are wrong: converting the entry into a closet to maximize storage and living area judges space by how much it holds, which is what paragraph 4 says we should not do; a front door opening straight into the kitchen is the collapsed sequence of paragraph 3, where every arrival is an intrusion or full admission; a glass-walled facade makes everything visible, which removes the privacy that lets the household keep its life out of view. Trap: Choosing a design that feels open and modern instead of one that preserves the in-between space.

qs.q: Which finding would most undermine the author's claim in paragraph 3?
o: Doorbell cameras are more common in homes without vestibules than in older homes that kept them.
Not quite. More cameras without vestibules supports the claim about compensating for the lost room.
Vestibules reduce winter heating costs in cold climates.
Not quite. Heating costs concern the airlock role in paragraph 2, not the social need in paragraph 3.
Residents of homes with and without vestibules answer the door equally often and with equal ease.
Correct: If both groups answer the door equally often and easily, there is no sign of an unmet need.
Many old homes with vestibules reflected class hierarchies.
Not quite. This is the author's concession in paragraph 4 and doesn't touch paragraph 3's claim.
qs.x: Correct: A 'weaken' question starts with the claim. Paragraph 3 says that without vestibules arrivals become 'an intrusion or a full admission,' that residents 'compensate' in awkward ways, and that this suggests the need still exists and is 'met badly.' If residents of homes with and without vestibules answered the door equally often and with equal ease, there would be no sign of an unmet need. Why the others are wrong: more doorbell cameras in homes without vestibules supports the claim, since cameras are one of the compensations; vestibules reducing winter heating costs concerns the airlock function from paragraph 2, not the social need in paragraph 3; old homes with vestibules reflecting class hierarchies is the author's own concession in paragraph 4 and doesn't affect paragraph 3. Trap: Choosing a fact that sounds related but supports the claim or concerns a different one.

passages.title: The Bedside and the Ledger
text: Histories of medicine like to stage a duel. On one side stands the old physician, who reads each patient as a singular case and trusts the trained intuition of his fingertips. On the other stands the statistician, who counts outcomes across hundreds of patients and lets the numbers speak. In the triumphal version of the story, the ledger wins, superstition retreats, and modern medicine is born. I think this version gets the winner right and the battle wrong.

Consider the Parisian physician Pierre Louis, who in the 1830s tallied the courses of pneumonia patients bled early or late and concluded that bloodletting did far less good than his colleagues believed. Louis is usually cast as the hero of the duel. Yet his opponents did not object to counting as such; many of them counted constantly, recording pulses, temperatures and fluid losses. What they resisted was the claim that an average drawn from many bodies could tell a physician what to do with the one body in front of him. That objection was not superstition. It was a serious question about how a general truth becomes a particular decision, and it has never been fully answered.

What the numerical method actually changed was not the amount of knowledge but its address. Before Louis, medical authority lived in the person of the experienced practitioner, who could not easily be contradicted by anyone who had not stood at the same bedsides. After him, authority increasingly lived in tables that anyone literate could inspect, dispute and extend. The ledger made medical knowledge portable, cumulative and public. That is a genuine achievement, but it is an achievement in the social organization of knowledge, not a victory of reason over unreason.

Seeing the change this way matters because the old question returns whenever we forget it. A clinician who applies a trial's average result to a frail ninety-year-old patient who resembles no one in the trial is facing exactly the difficulty Louis's critics raised. The honest response is neither to discard the ledger nor to worship it, but to admit that every application of a statistic to a person is an act of judgment, and to train that judgment as carefully as we once trained the fingertips.

qs.q: The author's central claim about the rise of the numerical method is that it primarily:
o: proved that clinical intuition had always been a form of superstition
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the critics' objection was a serious question, not superstition.
increased the total amount of reliable knowledge available to doctors
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says the method changed not the amount of knowledge but its address.
relocated medical authority from individual practitioners to shared, inspectable records
Correct: paragraph 3 says authority moved into tables that anyone could inspect, so knowledge became public.
ended the use of bloodletting in Parisian hospitals within a decade
Not quite. The passage gives Louis's conclusion but says nothing about how quickly practice changed.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the author's main claim about what the numerical method did. Paragraph 3 says it directly: the method changed not the amount of knowledge but its address. Before Louis, authority lived in the experienced practitioner; after him, it lived in tables anyone literate could inspect, dispute and extend. So authority moved from individual doctors to shared, public records. Why the others are wrong: proving intuition was superstition is contradicted by paragraph 2, which says the critics' objection was not superstition; increasing the total amount of reliable knowledge is the exact idea paragraph 3 denies; ending bloodletting in Paris within a decade goes beyond the passage, which gives Louis's conclusion but nothing about how fast practice changed. Trap: Picking the standard, triumphal reading of medical history that the author is arguing against.

qs.q: The author mentions that Louis's opponents 'counted constantly' (paragraph 2) most likely in order to:
o: show that the dispute was about applying averages, not about whether to count
Correct: paragraph 2 says the opponents resisted using an average to decide about one body, not counting itself.
suggest that Louis copied his method from his own critics
Not quite. The passage never says Louis borrowed his method from anyone.
demonstrate that the critics' data on bloodletting were more accurate than the figures Louis relied on
Not quite. The passage never compares how accurate the two sides' data were.
argue that bloodletting was in fact an effective treatment
Not quite. The author doesn't defend bloodletting. The point is about reasoning from averages to one patient.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks why the author mentions that Louis's opponents counted constantly. Read paragraph 2. It says the opponents did not object to counting as such; they recorded pulses, temperatures and fluid losses. What they resisted was using an average from many bodies to decide what to do with the one body in front of the doctor. So the detail shows the fight was about applying averages, not about counting. Why the others are wrong: Louis copying his method from critics is never said anywhere; claiming the critics' bloodletting data were more accurate invents a comparison the passage never makes; arguing that bloodletting worked defends a treatment the author never defends, since the point is about reasoning from averages. Trap: Reading extra claims into a detail, so that a small fact is stretched into a story the passage doesn't tell.

qs.q: Which phrase best captures the author's attitude toward the 'triumphal version' of medical history?
o: Complete endorsement of both its conclusion and its framing of the dispute
Not quite. The author rejects the duel framing, so this is not complete endorsement.
Complete rejection, since the old physicians were proved right about bloodletting
Not quite. The author says the ledger won and calls it a genuine achievement, so this isn't complete rejection.
Indifference, since historical narratives cannot affect practice
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says seeing the change correctly matters, so the author is not indifferent.
Partial agreement with its conclusion but rejection of its framing
Correct: paragraph 1 says the version gets the winner right and the battle wrong.
qs.x: Correct: This asks for the author's attitude toward the triumphal version of the story. Paragraph 1 gives it away in the last sentence: the triumphal version gets the winner right and the battle wrong. So the author agrees the ledger won, but rejects the picture of a duel between science and superstition. That is partial agreement with the conclusion and rejection of the framing. Why the others are wrong: complete endorsement ignores that the author rejects the duel framing; complete rejection because the old physicians were right about bloodletting fails, since the author grants that the ledger won and calls it a genuine achievement in paragraph 3; indifference fails because paragraph 4 says the framing matters, as the old question keeps returning in practice. Trap: Choosing an all-or-nothing attitude when the author's tone is split.

qs.q: Which modern situation most closely parallels the difficulty raised by Louis's critics?
o: Debating whether hospital records should be stored electronically or on paper
Not quite. How records are stored has nothing to do with applying a group average to one patient.
Deciding whether a drug tested only on young adults should be given to a child
Correct: like the frail patient in paragraph 4, the child resembles no one in the trial.
Determining whether a trial had enough participants to detect an effect of the size expected
Not quite. Trial size concerns whether the trial is valid, not how to apply its result to one person.
Choosing which journal should publish a large epidemiological study
Not quite. Which journal publishes a study is unrelated to the general-to-particular problem.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for a modern case that matches the critics' difficulty. First name that difficulty. Paragraph 2 says it is how a general truth drawn from many bodies becomes a decision about one particular body, and paragraph 4 gives the example of a frail ninety-year-old who resembles no one in the trial. A drug tested only on young adults being considered for a child is the same gap: the patient is unlike the group studied. Why the others are wrong: paper versus electronic records is about storage, not applying an average to a person; asking whether a trial had enough participants is about whether the trial itself is sound, not about using its result on one individual; choosing a journal has nothing to do with the problem. Trap: Choosing an answer that mentions medicine or studies without checking that it matches the exact problem.

qs.q: Suppose historians found that, after Louis, junior doctors began successfully challenging senior doctors by citing published tables. How would this affect the author's argument?
o: It would weaken the claim that the critics raised a serious question
Not quite. Who wins arguments doesn't show the critics' question about averages was unserious.
It would support the claim that numbers shifted where authority resided
Correct: paragraph 3 says tables let anyone literate dispute established practitioners, which is what this finding shows.
It would weaken the claim that the ledger made knowledge cumulative
Not quite. Citing published tables is an example of knowledge being shared and built on.
It would have no bearing, since the author discusses only Louis himself
Not quite. Paragraph 3 makes broad claims about how medical authority is organized, so this does bear on it.
qs.x: Correct: This asks how a new finding would affect the argument. Junior doctors successfully challenging seniors by citing published tables is evidence for paragraph 3's claim that after Louis, authority lived in tables anyone literate could inspect, dispute and extend. So it supports the idea that numbers shifted where authority sat. Why the others are wrong: weakening the claim that the critics raised a serious question fails because who wins an argument doesn't show whether averages fit individual patients; weakening the claim that the ledger made knowledge cumulative fails because citing published tables is knowledge being shared and built upon; saying it has no bearing is wrong since the author makes broad claims about how medical knowledge is socially organized, not only about Louis. Trap: Treating a finding that sounds new as automatically opposing the author.

qs.q: Which assumption is necessary for the author's recommendation in the final paragraph?
o: Clinical trials systematically exclude elderly patients on purpose to make their results look better
Not quite. The example only needs some patients to differ from the trial group, not deliberate exclusion.
Fingertip diagnosis was more accurate than statistical diagnosis
Not quite. The author never ranks fingertip diagnosis against statistical diagnosis.
Most clinicians already worship statistical averages
Not quite. The author warns against worshipping the ledger but doesn't assume most clinicians do.
Skill in applying statistics can be trained.
Correct: the author urges us to train that judgment, which assumes it can be trained.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for an assumption the final recommendation needs. A necessary assumption is one the argument falls apart without. Paragraph 4 says we should admit that applying a statistic to a person is an act of judgment and then train that judgment as carefully as we once trained the fingertips. Telling people to train something only makes sense if the skill can be trained. Why the others are wrong: trials deliberately excluding the elderly goes too far, because the example only needs some patients to differ from the trial group; fingertip diagnosis being more accurate is a ranking the author never makes; most clinicians worshipping averages isn't needed, since the author only warns against it. Trap: Picking a dramatic claim that would be nice for the author, when the real assumption is the quiet one inside the recommendation.

passages.title: What the Unbroken Shot Hides
text: Among critics who care about such things, there persists a moral hierarchy of film technique. The long take, a single shot that runs uncut for minutes, sits near the top: it is said to respect the spectator's freedom, to let time pass as it really passes, and to refuse the manipulation of editing. Montage, the rapid assembly of fragments, sits near the bottom, tainted by its association with propaganda and advertising. The long take is honest; the cut is a lie.

This hierarchy has a distinguished pedigree, but it confuses a style with a virtue. A long take is no less constructed than a montage sequence. Someone chose where the camera stands, what enters and leaves the frame, when the actors move and how long the shot will run before it ends. The absence of visible cuts does not remove the filmmaker's hand; it hides it. If anything, a carefully choreographed long take can be more coercive than editing, because the spectator, believing herself free to look wherever she likes, does not notice how thoroughly her attention has been steered by movement, light and sound.

Nor does montage necessarily deceive. A sequence that cuts between a factory owner's banquet and his workers' meager meal makes its argument openly. The juxtaposition announces itself; the viewer sees that a comparison is being made and can accept or reject it. Editing, in this sense, can be the more candid technique, since it wears its artifice on its surface.

None of this means that the long take lacks distinctive powers. Duration can produce effects nothing else can: the slow accumulation of tension, the boredom that turns into attention, the sense of a world continuing beyond the frame. My objection is only to the claim that these powers are ethical rather than aesthetic. Techniques do not carry morals within them. Honesty in film, as elsewhere, belongs to what is being said and to whether the speaker invites us to see how it is being said, not to the length of the sentences.

qs.q: The main purpose of the passage is to:
o: challenge the idea that long takes are more honest
Correct: paragraph 2 says the hierarchy confuses a style with a virtue.
argue that montage is aesthetically superior to the long take in every kind of film
Not quite. Paragraph 4 credits the long take with powers nothing else can produce, so the author doesn't rank montage above it.
trace the historical origins of montage in propaganda films
Not quite. Propaganda appears only in passing in paragraph 1.
explain the technical difficulty of filming a long take
Not quite. The passage is about ethics and style, not technical difficulty.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the main purpose of the whole passage. Paragraph 1 describes a hierarchy where the long take is honest and the cut is a lie. Paragraph 2 then answers that this hierarchy "confuses a style with a virtue." Paragraphs 3 and 4 keep building that case. So the purpose is to challenge the idea that long takes are more honest. Why the others are wrong: arguing that montage is better in every kind of film overshoots, because paragraph 4 says the long take has powers nothing else can produce; tracing montage's origins in propaganda grabs a passing mention from paragraph 1 and turns it into the topic; explaining the technical difficulty of filming a long take is never discussed, since the passage is about ethics and style. Trap: Choosing a choice that flips the author's view into its opposite, when the author only wants to knock down a claim.

qs.q: The banquet example in paragraph 3 is used chiefly to illustrate that:
o: a cut can openly present a comparison the viewer is free to evaluate
Correct: paragraph 3 says the juxtaposition announces itself, so the viewer can accept or reject it.
montage is most effective when it depicts economic injustice
Not quite. The author uses the example for how the cut works, not to rank political subjects.
long takes cannot depict two locations at the same time
Not quite. The passage never says this about long takes.
editing always manipulates viewers without their awareness, whatever the director intends
Not quite. This is the opposite of the point: the example shows editing being open about its comparison.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what the banquet-and-workers example is meant to show. Read paragraph 3: cutting between a factory owner's banquet and his workers' meager meal makes its argument openly. The juxtaposition announces itself, so the viewer sees a comparison is being made and can accept or reject it. The author's conclusion is that editing can be the more candid technique. Why the others are wrong: saying montage works best on economic injustice treats the example as being about its subject, when it is about how the argument is made; saying long takes cannot show two places at once is a claim the passage never makes; saying editing always manipulates viewers without their awareness is the opposite of the point, because here the editing is open. Trap: Getting caught up in the content of an example, rather than asking what point the author uses it to prove.

qs.q: According to the author, why can a long take be 'more coercive' than editing?
o: Long takes are longer and therefore exhaust the viewer's critical faculties before the scene ends
Not quite. The author blames hidden steering, not tiredness, for the coercion.
Viewers who feel free to look anywhere fail to notice how their gaze is directed
Correct: paragraph 2 says the spectator does not notice how her attention is steered.
Long takes are mostly used in propaganda and advertising
Not quite. Paragraph 1 links propaganda to montage, not to the long take.
Editing gives the viewer no choice about where to look, so the viewer notices the director's control
Not quite. That would make editing more coercive, the opposite of the author's point.
qs.x: Correct: This asks why the author says a long take can be more coercive than editing. The sentence is in paragraph 2. A carefully planned long take can steer the spectator by movement, light and sound, while she believes she is free to look wherever she likes. Because she thinks she is free, she does not notice how much her attention is being guided. Coercion here means hidden steering. Why the others are wrong: viewer exhaustion from length is tempting since long takes are long, but the author blames hidden steering, not fatigue; long takes being used mostly in propaganda is wrong because paragraph 1 ties propaganda to montage; editing giving the viewer no choice and so being noticed would make editing the more coercive one, which is backwards. Trap: Picking the explanation that sounds intuitive about the thing's name rather than the reason the author gives.

qs.q: Which statement would the author be most likely to accept?
o: The long take produces no effects that editing cannot also achieve
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says duration produces effects nothing else can.
Ethical filmmakers should avoid visible cuts whenever possible
Not quite. This repeats the hierarchy the author rejects.
A documentary that cuts frequently can be more truthful than one that never cuts
Correct: paragraph 4 says honesty lies in what is said and how openly, not in shot length.
Film techniques carry inherent moral qualities apart from their use
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says techniques do not carry morals within them.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks which statement the author would accept. Use paragraph 4: honesty belongs to what is being said and whether the speaker invites us to see how it is being said, not to the length of the sentences. So a documentary that cuts often could be more truthful than one that never cuts, because truth depends on content and openness, not on cutting. Why the others are wrong: the long take producing no effects editing cannot match contradicts paragraph 4, which says duration produces effects nothing else can; ethical filmmakers avoiding cuts restates the hierarchy the author rejects in paragraph 1; techniques carrying moral qualities apart from their use contradicts the line that techniques do not carry morals within them. Trap: Choosing a statement that sounds like a general film opinion rather than one that follows from the author's actual claim.

qs.q: Which analogy best reflects the author's reasoning about film technique?
o: A photograph is more honest than a painting because it involves no human choices
Not quite. The author says even an unedited image involves many human choices.
Handwritten letters are more sincere than typed ones because they show the writer's effort and care
Not quite. This ties virtue to a technique, which is the move the author rejects.
A live broadcast is more honest than a recording because it cannot be edited
Not quite. This repeats the long-take hierarchy the author disputes.
Short sentences are not truer than long ones; content decides.
Correct: the final sentence compares shot length to the length of sentences, and content decides truth.
qs.x: Correct: This asks for the analogy that matches the author's reasoning. The author's last line in paragraph 4 compares shot length to the length of sentences: honesty belongs to what is said, not to how long the sentences are. So the best parallel is that short sentences are not truer than long ones; content decides. Why the others are wrong: a photograph being more honest than a painting because it has no human choices clashes with paragraph 2, which says even an uncut shot involves many choices; handwritten letters being more sincere than typed ones links virtue to a technique, exactly what the author rejects; a live broadcast being more honest than a recording because it cannot be edited repeats the long-take hierarchy in a new costume. Trap: Falling for analogies that look different on the surface but quietly assume the very idea being argued against.

qs.q: A director makes a ten-minute uncut shot but adds an on-screen note explaining how each movement was rehearsed. How would the author most likely view this?
o: As destroying the long take's distinctive power of unbroken duration and immersion
Not quite. A note doesn't shorten the shot or remove its duration.
As pointless, since long takes are already fully honest
Not quite. The author denies that long takes are honest by nature, so the note isn't pointless.
As increasing the film's candor by showing how its effect is produced
Correct: paragraph 4 locates honesty partly in inviting us to see how it is being said.
As turning the long take into a form of montage
Not quite. A note adds no cuts or juxtaposed fragments, so it doesn't make the shot montage.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks how the author would view a ten-minute shot with an on-screen note about the rehearsal. Look at the last sentence of paragraph 4: honesty belongs to what is being said and to whether the speaker invites us to see how it is being said. A note explaining that each movement was rehearsed does exactly that, so the author would see it as making the film more candid. Why the others are wrong: destroying the long take's power fails because the note doesn't shorten the shot or end its duration; calling it pointless assumes long takes are already honest, which paragraph 2 denies; turning the long take into montage fails because no cuts or juxtaposed fragments are added. Trap: Treating an addition to the film as if it changed the technique itself.

passages.title: The Arrow and the Opening
text: Ancient Greek had two words for time. Chronos was time as sequence, the steady march of hours that a water clock could measure. Kairos was time as opportunity, the moment when an action becomes fitting or possible. The word seems to have been used of archery, where it named the narrow gap through which an arrow must pass, and of weaving, where it named the instant when the shuttle can slip through the parted threads. For the teachers of rhetoric, kairos named something no handbook could fully capture: the sense of when to speak, what to say to these listeners in this mood, and when to stop.

Modern instruction in persuasive writing has largely abandoned this idea. Students learn templates: a thesis in the first paragraph, three supporting points, a counterargument, a conclusion that restates the thesis. Such templates have real uses. They make arguments easier to grade and give beginners a scaffold. But they presuppose that a good argument is good everywhere, that its quality is a property of its internal structure rather than of its fit to an occasion.

The older tradition knew better. Gorgias, one of the first professional teachers of rhetoric, reportedly delighted in speaking on any subject an audience proposed, and his showpieces suggest a man more interested in responsiveness than in fixed rules. Even Aristotle, who did more than anyone to systematize rhetoric, insisted that the available means of persuasion must be discovered anew in each case. His categories of appeal were tools for noticing what a situation offered, not formulas for producing speeches in advance.

To restore kairos to the classroom would not mean discarding structure. It would mean teaching students to ask, before they write, who will read this, what those readers already believe, what has just happened that makes the topic urgent or tired, and what would be the wrong thing to say now. These questions cannot be answered by a template, which is precisely why they are worth teaching. An argument that is correct but untimely persuades no one, and an archer who aims perfectly at a closed gap still misses.

qs.q: As the passage uses the term, kairos refers to:
o: the fitting or opportune moment for an action
Correct: paragraph 1 defines kairos as time as opportunity, the fitting moment.
time measured as a steady sequence of hours and days
Not quite. Paragraph 1 gives that meaning to chronos, not kairos.
a standard structure for organizing an argument
Not quite. Templates are a modern practice the author contrasts with kairos.
Aristotle's list of the three types of appeal
Not quite. Paragraph 3 mentions Aristotle's categories but never calls them kairos.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what kairos means the way this passage uses it. Paragraph 1 sets two Greek words side by side. Chronos is time as sequence, the steady march of hours a water clock could measure. Kairos is time as opportunity, the moment when an action becomes fitting or possible, like the narrow gap an arrow must pass through. So kairos is the fitting or opportune moment. Why the others are wrong: time as a steady sequence of hours and days is the definition of chronos, given in the same paragraph; a standard structure for organizing an argument describes the templates in paragraph 2, which the author contrasts with kairos; Aristotle's list of appeals is mentioned in paragraph 3, but the passage never calls those categories kairos. Trap: Grabbing the definition from the wrong word when two terms are defined next to each other.

qs.q: The author's main criticism of writing templates is that they:
o: are too difficult for beginning writers to master
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says templates give beginners a helpful scaffold.
make it harder for instructors to grade student essays
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says templates make arguments easier to grade.
were invented by Gorgias and so reflect outdated thinking about how persuasion works
Not quite. Gorgias is shown as favoring responsiveness, not as inventing templates.
treat argumentative quality as independent of the audience and occasion
Correct: paragraph 2 says templates presuppose that quality is internal rather than fitted to an occasion.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the author's main criticism of templates. Start with paragraph 2. The author first grants real uses: templates are easier to grade and give beginners a scaffold. Then comes the complaint: they presuppose a good argument is good everywhere, that its quality comes from its internal structure rather than its fit to an occasion. So the criticism is that templates treat quality as independent of audience and occasion. Why the others are wrong: being too hard for beginners reverses what paragraph 2 says, that they help beginners; making grading harder also reverses it, since they make grading easier; saying Gorgias invented them is unsupported, because paragraph 3 shows Gorgias as someone who valued responsiveness over fixed rules. Trap: Choosing a criticism that sounds like a natural complaint, when the author has already conceded the opposite.

qs.q: The author refers to Aristotle in paragraph 3 most likely to show that:
o: Aristotle rejected Gorgias's interest in responding to audiences
Not quite. The passage describes no disagreement between Aristotle and Gorgias.
even the great systematizer of rhetoric treated persuasion as situational
Correct: paragraph 3 says Aristotle held that the means of persuasion must be discovered anew in each case.
systematic approaches to rhetoric inevitably fail
Not quite. The author calls Aristotle's categories tools for noticing, not failures.
modern templates are directly derived from Aristotle's categories of ethos, pathos, and logos
Not quite. The passage draws no line from Aristotle's categories to modern templates.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks why the author brings up Aristotle in paragraph 3. The paragraph says he did more than anyone to systematize rhetoric, yet he insisted that the available means of persuasion must be discovered anew in each case, and that his categories were tools for noticing what a situation offered. That is a surprising fact: even the great organizer treated persuasion as situational. Why the others are wrong: Aristotle rejecting Gorgias's responsiveness invents a disagreement the passage never describes; systematic approaches inevitably failing overreaches, because Aristotle's categories are called useful tools; modern templates deriving from ethos, pathos, and logos draws a line of descent the passage never draws, and in fact says Aristotle's categories were not formulas for producing speeches in advance. Trap: Choosing the dramatic answer, like a feud or a total failure, over the modest point that fits the text.

qs.q: Which practice would best fit the author's proposal for restoring kairos to the classroom?
o: Requiring every essay to place its thesis in the first sentence
Not quite. A first-sentence thesis rule is a fixed template, which is what the author critiques.
Having students rewrite one argument for two audiences with different prior beliefs
Correct: paragraph 4 urges students to ask who will read this and what those readers already believe.
Grading essays solely on grammar and spelling
Not quite. Grammar-only grading ignores the occasion and audience entirely.
Having students memorize famous ancient speeches word for word and deliver them before the class
Not quite. Memorizing old speeches repeats past occasions instead of fitting new ones.
qs.x: Correct: This asks which classroom practice fits the author's proposal. Paragraph 4 says restoring kairos means teaching students to ask who will read this, what those readers already believe, what has just happened, and what would be the wrong thing to say now. Having students rewrite one argument for two audiences with different prior beliefs puts exactly those questions into practice. Why the others are wrong: requiring the thesis in the first sentence is a fixed template rule, the approach the author critiques in paragraph 2; grading only on grammar and spelling ignores audience and occasion entirely; memorizing famous ancient speeches sounds faithful to the classical tradition, but it copies past occasions rather than fitting a new one. Trap: Choosing the answer that sounds classical or old-fashioned instead of the one that practices the questions the author lists.

qs.q: A speechwriter delivers a well-argued case for a budget cut the day after a disaster that the cut would have worsened, and the audience reacts with anger. The author would most likely explain the failure as:
o: proof that the argument's structure was logically flawed
Not quite. The case is stated to be well argued, and the author separates timing from structure.
evidence that audiences cannot be persuaded by reasoned argument once their emotions are aroused
Not quite. The author thinks timely arguments can persuade. The problem is fit, not reason.
a result of following Aristotle's categories too closely
Not quite. The author presents Aristotle's categories as tools for noticing situations.
a failure of timing, regardless of the argument's internal quality
Correct: paragraph 4 says a correct but untimely argument persuades no one.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks how the author would explain a speechwriter's failure. The case is stipulated to be well argued, so the structure and logic are not the problem. The failure is that it was delivered the day after a disaster, which makes it the wrong moment.
