Paragraph 4 gives the lesson: "An argument that is correct but untimely persuades no one," like an archer aiming perfectly at a closed gap. So it is a failure of timing. Why the others are wrong: a logical flaw ignores that the case was described as well argued, and the author separates timing from internal quality; audiences being unpersuadable by reason once emotional contradicts the author, who says fit, not reason, is the issue; following Aristotle's categories too closely is unsupported, since the author presents them as tools for noticing a situation. Trap: Blaming the argument when the story has already told you the argument was fine.

passages.title: Hot Iron and Reasonable Doubt
text: Few legal practices strike modern readers as more absurd than the medieval ordeal. An accused person might be made to carry a red-hot iron for several paces or plunge an arm into boiling water; if the wound healed cleanly after a few days, God had declared the person innocent. It is tempting to treat such procedures as pure superstition, a grim curiosity from an age before reason. I want to suggest that they were, within their world, a surprisingly shrewd solution to a problem every legal system faces.

That problem is what to do when evidence runs out. Where there were no witnesses and no confession, early medieval courts had few tools for discovering the truth. The ordeal was reserved for exactly such cases. Crucially, it worked through the beliefs of the accused. Someone who believed that God would reveal guilt had strong reason to confess or settle before ever touching the iron, while an innocent person, confident of vindication, had reason to proceed. The ordeal thus sorted defendants by their own expectations, and the mere prospect of it may have extracted many confessions from the guilty.

Records also suggest that a surprisingly large share of those who underwent the ordeal were cleared. One plausible explanation is that the priests who administered it had considerable discretion, over how hot the iron was, how long it was held and how a healing wound was judged, and may have tended to exonerate those who had shown willingness to proceed. If so, the ordeal was not blind chance but a ritual whose outcome reflected a reasonable inference: those willing to face it were probably innocent.

The system depended entirely on shared belief, and that is why it collapsed. In 1215 the Fourth Lateran Council forbade clergy to take part in ordeals, partly from theological doubts about demanding miracles of God. Without priests, the ritual lost its authority. English courts turned increasingly to juries of neighbors, a change usually told as progress. Perhaps it was. But we should notice that the jury, too, is a device for producing a verdict when certainty is unavailable, and that it, too, rests on a shared faith, in this case faith in the judgment of ordinary people.

qs.q: According to the passage, ordeals were typically used when:
o: the accused was a member of the clergy
Not quite. Priests administered ordeals. The passage doesn't say they were the accused.
a jury of neighbors could not agree on a verdict after hearing all the testimony
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says juries came after ordeals were abandoned.
the crime carried the death penalty and a jury refused to convict
Not quite. The passage never ties the ordeal to the severity of punishment.
no witnesses or confession were available to settle the case
Correct: paragraph 2 says the ordeal was reserved for cases where evidence ran out.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks when ordeals were typically used. Paragraph 2 says the problem was what to do when evidence runs out: with no witnesses and no confession, early medieval courts had few tools, and the ordeal was reserved for exactly such cases. Why the others are wrong: the accused being a member of the clergy is not mentioned, since priests administered ordeals but were not described as the accused; a jury failing to agree reverses the order of events, because paragraph 4 says juries came in after ordeals ended; the crime carrying the death penalty and a jury refusing to convict ties the ordeal to punishment severity and to juries, neither of which appears in the passage. Trap: Importing a familiar legal scenario from outside the passage instead of using the condition the author names.

qs.q: The author's argument that the ordeal 'sorted defendants by their own expectations' depends on the assumption that:
o: priests were indifferent to the outcome of each ordeal
Not quite. Paragraph 3 suggests priests used discretion, so indifference isn't assumed.
most accused persons sincerely believed God would reveal the truth
Correct: the sorting in paragraph 2 only works if the accused shared the belief that God would reveal the truth.
guilty people were physically less able to endure pain
Not quite. The mechanism concerns belief and choice, not pain tolerance.
juries would have reached the same verdicts as ordeals if they had been given the same cases
Not quite. The sorting argument doesn't depend on any comparison with juries.
qs.x: Correct: This asks for the assumption behind the sorting argument. Paragraph 2 says someone who believed God would reveal guilt had strong reason to confess or settle before touching the iron, while an innocent person, confident of vindication, would proceed. That only works if most accused people sincerely believed God would reveal the truth. Take away the belief and nobody has a reason to sort themselves. Why the others are wrong: priests being indifferent is not assumed, since paragraph 3 suggests they used discretion; guilty people being less able to endure pain is a physical explanation, but the mechanism here is belief and choice; juries reaching the same verdicts would compare two systems, which the sorting argument doesn't need. Trap: Choosing an assumption that sounds like it supports the ordeal, instead of the one the specific mechanism cannot work without.

qs.q: Which evidence from the passage best supports the claim that ordeal outcomes reflected 'a reasonable inference' rather than chance?
o: The Fourth Lateran Council forbade clergy participation in 1215
Not quite. The 1215 ban explains the ordeal's end, not how its outcomes were reached.
A large share of those who underwent the ordeal were cleared
Correct: paragraph 3 ties frequent acquittals to priests' discretion favoring those willing to proceed.
The accused might carry a red-hot iron for several paces
Not quite. This describes the procedure, not evidence about its outcomes.
English courts later turned to juries of neighbors
Not quite. Juries are the later system and say nothing about the logic of ordeal verdicts.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what evidence best supports the claim that ordeal outcomes reflected a reasonable inference, not chance. Paragraph 3 starts from records showing a surprisingly large share of those who underwent the ordeal were cleared. The author then suggests priests had discretion and tended to clear those who showed willingness to proceed, so the result reflected a sensible inference. The high rate of acquittals is the evidence. Why the others are wrong: the 1215 ban on clergy taking part explains how the system ended, not how verdicts were reached; carrying a red-hot iron for several paces describes the procedure, not what the outcomes showed; the later turn to juries concerns the next system. Trap: Choosing an interesting fact from the passage that doesn't actually address the claim being tested.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the replacement of ordeals by juries is best described as:
o: enthusiastic, viewing juries as wholly rational
Not quite. The author stresses that juries also rest on faith.
hostile, arguing that ordeals were more accurate than the juries that replaced them
Not quite. The author never claims ordeals were more accurate than juries.
indifferent, treating the change as unimportant
Not quite. The author draws a pointed parallel, which isn't indifference.
cautious, allowing progress but noting a likeness
Correct: paragraph 4 says perhaps it was progress, then notes juries too rest on shared faith.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the author's attitude toward replacing ordeals with juries. In paragraph 4, the author says the change is usually told as progress and answers "Perhaps it was." That is a hedge. Then the author points out that the jury is also a device for producing a verdict when certainty is unavailable, and also rests on shared faith. So the attitude is cautious: allowing progress but noting a likeness. Why the others are wrong: enthusiastic and wholly rational ignores the author's point that juries rest on faith; hostile, with ordeals more accurate, claims something the author never says; indifferent treats the change as unimportant, but the author draws a pointed parallel, which shows real interest. Trap: Picking a strong emotion when a mild, balanced tone is what the wording shows.

qs.q: Which modern practice works most like the mechanism the author attributes to the ordeal?
o: A lie-detector test whose main value is that suspects who believe it works confess beforehand
Correct: like the ordeal in paragraph 2, it works through the suspect's belief in its power.
A DNA test that matches crime-scene samples to a suspect who has denied being present at the scene
Not quite. DNA evidence works independently of what the suspect believes.
A jury trial in which twelve citizens weigh the evidence
Not quite. Paragraph 4 presents juries as a successor resting on faith in ordinary judgment.
A judge's sentencing guidelines based on prior convictions and the seriousness of the current offense
Not quite. Sentencing guidelines don't draw out confessions through the defendant's beliefs.
qs.x: Correct: This asks for a modern practice that works like the ordeal's mechanism. Paragraph 2 says the ordeal worked through the beliefs of the accused: those who believed God would reveal guilt had reason to confess or settle before the test, and the mere prospect of it may have extracted confessions. A lie-detector test valued mainly because suspects who believe it works confess beforehand works the same way. Why the others are wrong: a DNA match works regardless of what the suspect believes; a jury trial is described in paragraph 4 as the successor system that rests on faith in ordinary people's judgment, not on the suspect's beliefs; sentencing guidelines apply after a verdict and do nothing to draw out confessions. Trap: Choosing the modern tool that sounds most like finding truth, when the question is about how the process gets people to act.

passages.title: Reading the Rubbish Heap
text: The public imagines archaeology as a search for treasure: gold masks, painted tombs, the palaces of kings. Practicing archaeologists know that their most informative finds usually come from somewhere far less glamorous. A midden, the heap where a household or village dumped its refuse, can reveal what people ate, which animals they kept, what tools broke and were discarded, and how all of this changed over generations, layer upon layer.

The great virtue of garbage is that it was not meant to be seen. A monument is a message composed for an audience, often for posterity; it tells us what its builders wished to be remembered for. A trash heap tells us what they actually did. A king's inscription may boast of plenty while the village midden from the same decade fills with the bones of animals that were eaten only in famine. Where the two disagree, the archaeologist has good reason to trust the rubbish.

Yet garbage has biases of its own, and they are easy to forget precisely because no one intended them. Bone, pottery and stone survive for thousands of years; wood, textiles, leather and most plant foods rot within decades unless conditions are unusually dry, cold or waterlogged. A midden may therefore suggest a diet dominated by meat and shellfish simply because those remains endure while the grains, roots and greens that fed people daily have vanished. The absence of evidence in a trash heap is often evidence only of decay.

The lesson is not that rubbish is unreliable but that its honesty is of a particular kind. It is free from the distortions of intention but not from the distortions of chemistry. A careful archaeologist reads a midden the way a careful historian reads a chronicle: alert to what the source could not have recorded, as well as to what it does. Modern techniques, from sieving for tiny seeds to analyzing chemical residues in pottery, have begun to recover some of what decay erased. But the first discipline remains a habit of mind, the refusal to mistake what has survived for what once existed.

qs.q: According to the passage, why might a midden overrepresent meat in an ancient diet?
o: Bones survive far longer than most plant remains
Correct: paragraph 3 says bone endures while grains, roots and greens rot.
Ancient people deliberately buried plant waste elsewhere
Not quite. The passage blames decay, not deliberate disposal.
Kings exaggerated meat consumption in their inscriptions
Not quite. Inscriptions are discussed separately and don't shape midden contents.
Archaeologists have historically ignored animal bones
Not quite. Ignoring bones would make meat look rarer, not more common.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks why a midden might overrepresent meat in an ancient diet. Paragraph 3 explains it: bone, pottery and stone survive for thousands of years, while wood, textiles, leather and most plant foods rot within decades. So the grains, roots and greens that fed people daily vanish, and the midden seems meat-heavy. Why the others are wrong: burying plant waste elsewhere would be intentional disposal, but the passage blames decay, which no one intended; kings exaggerating meat consumption in inscriptions is a separate source from paragraph 2 and doesn't shape what is inside a midden; archaeologists ignoring animal bones would make meat look less common, the opposite effect. Trap: Looking for a human cause such as lying or neglect, when the passage names a physical one.

qs.q: The author contrasts a king's inscription with a village midden (paragraph 2) in order to show that:
o: inscriptions are always false while middens are always true, whatever their date or location
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says middens have biases too, so neither source is always reliable.
unintended remains can correct the self-presentation of deliberate records
Correct: paragraph 2 says trash shows what people did while monuments show what they wished remembered.
famines were more common than historians once believed
Not quite. The famine example illustrates conflicting sources, not how often famines happened.
villages kept better records than royal courts
Not quite. A midden isn't a record anyone kept. Its value is that no one intended it.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what the king's inscription versus the village midden contrast shows. Paragraph 2 says a monument is a message composed for an audience, telling us what builders wished to be remembered for, while a trash heap tells us what they actually did. The boasting-of-plenty example shows a midden correcting a deliberate record. Why the others are wrong: inscriptions always being false and middens always true overreaches, because paragraph 3 says middens have biases of their own; famines being more common than believed treats an example as a statistic, when it only shows two sources disagreeing; villages keeping better records than royal courts is wrong since a midden is not a record anyone kept. Trap: Turning a contrast into an absolute claim, like always or never.

qs.q: The author's statement that rubbish is free from 'the distortions of intention but not from the distortions of chemistry' means that middens:
o: were deliberately arranged to mislead later archaeologists
Not quite. That would be a distortion of intention, which the author says middens lack.
can only be studied using modern chemical analysis
Not quite. Here chemistry means decay, and paragraph 4 calls the first discipline a habit of mind.
are not shaped by a wish to impress yet are filtered by unequal preservation
Correct: paragraph 4 contrasts the absence of intent with the decay described in paragraph 3.
contain toxic substances that endanger excavators
Not quite. The phrase is about preservation bias, not physical hazards.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what free from the distortions of intention but not from the distortions of chemistry means. Distortions of intention come from people shaping a message, like a king's inscription in paragraph 2. Garbage was not made to impress anyone, so it has none. But chemistry is decay, as paragraph 3 explains: bone survives while plants and cloth rot. So a midden isn't shaped by a wish to impress, yet it is filtered by unequal preservation. Why the others are wrong: deliberately arranged to mislead would be a distortion of intention, which middens lack; only studied with modern chemical analysis misreads chemistry as a tool, and paragraph 4 calls the first discipline a habit of mind; toxic substances endangering excavators misreads the phrase as a physical hazard. Trap: Taking chemistry literally as lab work instead of the decay process.

qs.q: Which situation best illustrates the 'habit of mind' the author recommends?
o: Concluding that a site's people ate no vegetables because no plant remains were found in its midden
Not quite. This treats absence caused by decay as real absence, the error paragraph 3 warns against.
Trusting a royal inscription over a midden because it is written and was meant to be read by later generations
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the archaeologist has reason to trust the rubbish when the two disagree.
Excavating only tombs because they contain the most valuable artifacts
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says the most informative finds come from middens, not treasure.
Concluding that a lack of wooden tools at a dry-rotted site does not prove none were used
Correct: it refuses to mistake what survived for what existed, as paragraph 4 urges.
qs.x: Correct: This asks which situation shows the habit of mind from paragraph 4: "the refusal to mistake what has survived for what once existed." Concluding that a lack of wooden tools at a site where wood rots does not prove none were used is that habit: it refuses to treat missing evidence as proof of absence. Why the others are wrong: concluding that no vegetables were eaten because no plant remains were found makes the exact mistake paragraph 3 warns about, absence due to decay; trusting a royal inscription over a midden contradicts paragraph 2, where the archaeologist has good reason to trust the rubbish when the two disagree; excavating only tombs for valuable artifacts is the treasure-hunting idea paragraph 1 says practicing archaeologists reject. Trap: Choosing an answer that sounds careful or scholarly but actually makes the error the passage warns about.

qs.q: At a waterlogged site, excavators find a midden full of preserved seeds and textile fragments. Compared with a typical dry midden, this site would most likely:
o: show a diet more dominated by meat and shellfish
Not quite. Preserved plants would reduce, not increase, meat's apparent dominance.
be less useful because it lacks a deliberate message
Not quite. All middens lack deliberate messages, and the author counts this as a virtue.
give a fuller picture of daily plant use
Correct: paragraph 3 says waterlogged conditions can preserve normally perishable remains.
contradict the claim that garbage was not meant to be seen by anyone outside the household
Not quite. Preservation conditions have nothing to do with why the refuse was thrown out.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what a waterlogged midden with preserved seeds and textiles would give compared with a typical dry midden. Paragraph 3 says wood, textiles, leather and most plant foods rot unless conditions are unusually dry, cold or waterlogged. A waterlogged site keeps those perishable remains, so it offsets the usual bias and gives a fuller picture of daily plant use. Why the others are wrong: a diet looking more dominated by meat would be the effect of losing plants, but here plants survive, so meat would look less dominant; being less useful for lacking a deliberate message fails, because every midden lacks one and the author counts that as a virtue; contradicting the claim that garbage wasn't meant to be seen confuses preservation with original intent. Trap: Reversing the effect of preservation, so that better survival of plants seems to push the picture toward meat.

passages.title: The Eloquence of Blank Space
text: Historians of cartography once told a simple story about the empty spaces on maps. Medieval and Renaissance mapmakers, the story went, filled unknown regions with sea serpents, cannibal kings and fanciful mountain ranges because they could not bear to admit ignorance; modern cartographers, chastened by science, learned to leave the unknown blank. The blank, on this account, is a badge of honesty, the visible trace of a discipline that has learned to say only what it can verify.

This story flatters us, and it is mostly wrong. Decorative monsters did not usually stand in for ignorance; they often marked waters that sailors had reported as dangerous, and the elaborate cartouches that filled interior spaces advertised the wealth of a patron rather than making a claim about terrain. More importantly, the blank that replaced them was not a neutral confession. When eighteenth-century European mapmakers stripped the interiors of Africa and the Americas of the towns and rivers their predecessors had copied from travelers’ reports, they did not merely subtract error. They also erased knowledge that Indigenous guides and traders had supplied, knowledge that did not count because it had not been measured by a European instrument.

The blank, then, was a standard of evidence masquerading as modesty. It declared that a place was unknown until a particular kind of person had surveyed it, and in doing so it turned inhabited land into an open invitation. A space marked as empty on a map is easier to imagine as empty on the ground; the rhetoric of scientific caution doubled as a rhetoric of availability. It is no accident that the great age of the blank coincided with the great age of territorial claiming.

None of this means that the older maps were better. Their monsters misled, and their borrowed rivers sometimes flowed in impossible directions. The point is that every map makes choices about what counts as knowing, and those choices are never purely technical. To read a map well is to ask not only what it shows but whose testimony it was willing to believe.

qs.q: The author’s central claim about the blank spaces on eighteenth-century maps is that they:
o: reflected a selective standard of evidence with political consequences
Correct: paragraph 3 calls the blank a standard of evidence masquerading as modesty that made land seem available.
were an honest admission of ignorance that improved accuracy and had no political consequences
Not quite. This is the old story paragraph 2 rejects as flattering and mostly wrong.
were less accurate than the decorated maps they replaced
Not quite. Paragraph 4 explicitly denies that the older maps were better.
were introduced chiefly to lower the cost of engraving the copper printing plates
Not quite. The passage never discusses production costs. It explains the blank through evidence and power.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the author's central claim about the blank spaces on eighteenth-century maps. Paragraph 3 states it: the blank was "a standard of evidence masquerading as modesty." It declared a place unknown until a particular kind of person had surveyed it, and so it made inhabited land look like an open invitation. So the blank reflected a selective standard of evidence with political consequences. Why the others are wrong: an honest admission of ignorance with no political consequences is the flattering story paragraph 2 calls mostly wrong; being less accurate than decorated maps goes against paragraph 4, which says none of this means older maps were better; lowering engraving costs is never mentioned, since the passage explains the blank through evidence and power. Trap: Choosing the view the author sets up in paragraph 1 only to knock it down.

qs.q: According to paragraph 2, the sea monsters on older maps often:
o: concealed the mapmaker’s ignorance of the coastline
Not quite. That is the old story. Paragraph 2 says monsters did not usually stand in for ignorance.
advertised the wealth of the map’s patron
Not quite. Paragraph 2 gives that job to the cartouches, not the monsters.
marked waters sailors reported as dangerous
Correct: paragraph 2 says monsters often marked waters sailors reported as dangerous.
recorded information supplied by Indigenous guides to the mapmakers
Not quite. Paragraph 2 links Indigenous knowledge to interior towns and rivers, not sea monsters.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what paragraph 2 says the sea monsters often did. The sentence is: "Decorative monsters did not usually stand in for ignorance; they often marked waters that sailors had reported as dangerous." So the monsters often marked waters sailors reported as dangerous. Why the others are wrong: concealing the mapmaker's ignorance is the old story of paragraph 1 that paragraph 2 corrects; advertising a patron's wealth is tempting because it sits in the same sentence, but the passage gives that job to the elaborate cartouches that filled interior spaces; recording information from Indigenous guides is tied in paragraph 2 to towns and rivers in the interiors of Africa and the Americas, not to sea monsters. Trap: Matching a claim to the wrong noun when two decorative features are described close together.

qs.q: The author mentions that older maps had rivers flowing “in impossible directions” most likely in order to:
o: show that travelers' reports were generally unreliable and should have been discarded
Not quite. The author defends the value of reported knowledge. One flaw isn't a verdict on all reports.
concede the flaws of older maps without giving up the main argument
Correct: paragraph 4 grants that older maps misled, then restates that every map embeds choices about knowing.
argue that instrument-based surveys were unnecessary for producing accurate maps
Not quite. Admitting older errors, if anything, shows measurement had value.
prove that monsters were more trustworthy than rivers
Not quite. The author says both monsters and borrowed rivers could mislead and ranks neither.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks why the author mentions rivers flowing in impossible directions. It appears at the start of paragraph 4: "None of this means that the older maps were better. Their monsters misled, and their borrowed rivers sometimes flowed in impossible directions." That is a concession. The author admits the older maps had flaws, then returns to the main point that every map makes choices about what counts as knowing. Why the others are wrong: showing that travelers' reports were unreliable and should be discarded works against the author, whose whole case is that such testimony was wrongly dropped; arguing that instrument-based surveys were unnecessary reverses the point, since admitting older errors if anything shows measurement had value; proving monsters more trustworthy than rivers fails because the author says both misled. Trap: Reading a concession as the main argument.

qs.q: The claim that it is “no accident” that the age of the blank coincided with territorial claiming depends most on which assumption?
o: Governments ordered mapmakers to erase Indigenous knowledge on purpose.
Not quite. The author argues from effect, not from a deliberate order. That claim is stronger than needed.
How land is represented can shape how people think about taking it.
Correct: paragraph 3 says land shown as empty is easier to imagine as empty on the ground.
Indigenous reports were always more accurate than European surveys.
Not quite. The argument is about which testimony counted, not that one source was always more accurate.
A territory cannot be claimed until it has been fully surveyed.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 suggests the opposite: unsurveyed blank land invited claims.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what assumption the no accident claim depends on. The author links two things, blank maps and territorial claiming, so there must be a bridge between them. Paragraph 3 supplies it: a space marked as empty on a map is easier to imagine as empty on the ground. So the assumption is that how land is represented can shape how people think about taking it. Why the others are wrong: governments ordering Indigenous knowledge erased on purpose is stronger than the argument needs, since the author argues from effect and never claims a documented order; Indigenous reports always being more accurate than European surveys is wrong because the argument is about whose testimony counted, not who was always right; a territory not being claimable until fully surveyed is the opposite of paragraph 3, where unsurveyed blank land invited claims. Trap: Choosing the most dramatic claim, like a conspiracy, when the argument needs only a modest link.

qs.q: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author’s account of why interiors were left blank?
o: Some medieval monsters appeared in waters no sailor had ever visited.
Not quite. This touches a side point about older maps, not the eighteenth-century blanks.
Eighteenth-century survey instruments were more precise than earlier ones.
Not quite. This is consistent with the passage and doesn't explain away the exclusion of testimony.
Eighteenth-century mapmakers often kept Indigenous-reported rivers that no European had measured.
Correct: paragraph 2 says such knowledge was erased for lacking European measurement, and this contradicts that.
Patrons continued to commission decorated cartouches in that century.
Not quite. Cartouches are a decorative detail and bear little on why interiors went blank.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks which finding would most weaken the author's explanation of the blank interiors. In paragraph 2, the author says mapmakers erased towns and rivers that Indigenous guides and traders supplied because that knowledge had not been measured by a European instrument. If mapmakers often kept Indigenous-reported rivers that no European had measured, then that cause collapses. Why the others are wrong: medieval monsters in waters no sailor visited touches only a side point about older maps; more precise eighteenth-century instruments fits the passage and doesn't explain away the exclusion of testimony; patrons still commissioning cartouches concerns a decorative detail and doesn't bear on why interiors went blank. Trap: Choosing a finding about maps in general instead of the one that attacks the author's central cause.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author’s view of the cartographic blank?
o: A star chart leaves gaps where no telescope has yet looked.
Not quite. This matches the honest-blank story of paragraph 1, since no available testimony is excluded.
A species database lists a fish as absent from a lake until a credentialed scientist logs it, despite local fishers’ reports.
Correct: like the blank in paragraph 3, the absence reflects whose testimony counts, not what is actually there.
A tourist map highlights only attractions that paid for advertising.
Not quite. This resembles the patron-driven cartouches, a minor point, not the blank's exclusion of testimony.
A weather map shows forecasts but omits last year’s rainfall.
Not quite. Leaving out irrelevant data isn't the same as discounting knowledgeable informants.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the situation closest to the author's view of the blank. The author's point, from paragraphs 2 and 3, is that a blank doesn't just show what is unknown; it shows whose testimony was accepted, and so makes a place seem empty. A database that lists a fish as absent from a lake until a credentialed scientist logs it, despite local fishers' reports, does the same: the absence comes from a rule about who counts. Why the others are wrong: a star chart with gaps where no telescope has looked matches the honest-blank story of paragraph 1, because no available testimony is being thrown out; a tourist map with only paid attractions resembles the patron-driven cartouches, a minor point; a weather map omitting last year's rainfall leaves out irrelevant data, not knowledgeable informants. Trap: Choosing the example that looks most like a map with gaps instead of the one with the same logic.

passages.title: The Tale Without an Original
text: When nineteenth-century collectors went into the countryside to record folktales, they believed they were rescuing something old and fragile: the authentic voice of the people, preserved by oral tradition and threatened by literacy and the city. Their published volumes presented the tales as found objects, faithfully transcribed. We now know that many collectors polished what they heard, merging versions from different tellers, cutting coarse episodes, adding moral reflections and, in some cases, relying on informants who were themselves well-read members of the middle class.

It is tempting to respond to these revelations with disillusionment, to conclude that the collections are forgeries and that the true folktale lies somewhere behind them, uncontaminated. But this response repeats the collectors’ own error. It assumes that there was once a pure, original version of each tale, and that every later telling is a degradation of it. Oral tradition does not work that way. A tale exists only in its performances, and each teller adapts it to an audience, a season and a purpose. There is no first telling to recover, only a cloud of variants, none of which has a stronger claim than the others to be the tale itself.

Seen in this light, the collector who edited a story was not stepping outside tradition but taking part in it. He was one more teller, adapting the material for a new audience, the reading public, as village storytellers had adapted it for the hearth. His version differs from theirs in its medium and its reach, not in its basic relationship to some lost source.

This does not excuse the collectors’ claims of fidelity, which misled readers about what they were getting. The problem was not that they changed the tales; it was that they denied changing them. The honest folklorist today records the variants, names the tellers, and admits her own hand in shaping the record.

qs.q: How does the author respond to the discovery that collectors edited the tales they published?
o: The collections are forgeries that hide the true folktales.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 rejects this disillusioned response as repeating the collectors' error.
The editing was harmless because readers knew the tales had been changed.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says the claims of fidelity misled readers.
Scholars should reconstruct each tale’s original version.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says there is no first telling to recover.
The claims of fidelity were wrong, but the editing itself continued oral tradition.
Correct: paragraph 3 calls the editor one more teller and paragraph 4 faults only the denial of changes.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks how the author responds to the discovery that collectors edited the tales. The answer has two halves. Paragraph 3 says an editing collector was not stepping outside tradition but taking part in it, as one more teller adapting the tale for a new audience. Paragraph 4 says the fault was not that they changed the tales but that they denied changing them. So the claims of fidelity were wrong, but the editing itself continued oral tradition. Why the others are wrong: calling the collections forgeries hiding true folktales is the disillusioned reaction paragraph 2 says repeats the collectors' error; saying editing was harmless because readers knew is false, since paragraph 4 says readers were misled; reconstructing each tale's original contradicts paragraph 2, where there is no first telling to recover. Trap: Choosing an answer that captures only half of a two-part position.

qs.q: The phrase “a cloud of variants” in paragraph 2 primarily emphasizes that:
o: no version of a tale is the true original
Correct: paragraph 2 says no variant has a stronger claim than the others to be the tale itself.
the tales were vague and hard to transcribe
Not quite. The image concerns many equal versions, not vague content.
the oldest versions have been lost forever
Not quite. The author denies there was a single first version to lose.
collectors confused tales from different regions and villages
Not quite. The phrase describes oral tradition itself, not collectors' mistakes.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks what a cloud of variants emphasizes. Paragraph 2 says a tale exists only in its performances, and "there is no first telling to recover, only a cloud of variants, none of which has a stronger claim than the others to be the tale itself." The image of a cloud, with no center and no outline, stresses many equal versions and no true original. Why the others are wrong: the tales being vague and hard to transcribe confuses a cloud of versions with blurry content; the oldest versions being lost forever is backward, since the author denies there was ever a single first version to lose; collectors confusing tales from different regions turns a description of oral tradition into a complaint about collectors. Trap: Picking the choice that pulls a literal meaning out of the picture of a cloud (fuzzy, vanishing) instead of what the author says it shows.

qs.q: According to paragraph 1, which practice did some collectors engage in?
o: Recording tellers with early sound equipment
Not quite. The passage never mentions sound recording.
Merging versions told by different storytellers
Correct: paragraph 1 lists merging versions from different tellers.
Paying storytellers to invent new tales for them
Not quite. Paragraph 1 describes polishing tales, not commissioning inventions.
Translating foreign tales and passing them off as local
Not quite. No such practice is described in paragraph 1.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks which practice paragraph 1 says some collectors engaged in. It lists them: they "polished what they heard, merging versions from different tellers, cutting coarse episodes, adding moral reflections," and in some cases relied on informants who were well-read middle-class people. Merging versions told by different storytellers is named directly. Why the others are wrong: recording tellers with early sound equipment is never mentioned; paying storytellers to invent new tales for them describes inventing, but the paragraph describes polishing existing tales; translating foreign tales and passing them off as local is a plausible abuse, but it appears nowhere in the passage. Trap: Choosing a believable editing sin from imagination instead of the ones the paragraph lists.

qs.q: The author would most likely criticize a modern folklorist who:
o: publishes several variants of a tale with tellers named
Not quite. Paragraph 4 describes this as the honest folklorist's practice.
adapts a tale for children and notes in a preface the changes she made
Not quite. Paragraph 3 treats adapting as tradition, and noting changes meets paragraph 4's honesty standard.
publishes one composite tale as a single teller’s exact words
Correct: paragraph 4 faults denying changes, which presenting a composite as one teller's exact words does.
describes her own role in shaping the record
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says the honest folklorist admits her own hand.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks which modern folklorist the author would criticize. Paragraph 4 puts the fault in denying changes, not in making them: the honest folklorist records the variants, names the tellers, and admits her own hand. A folklorist who publishes one composite tale as a single teller's exact words hides the merging and so repeats the collectors' denial. Why the others are wrong: publishing several variants with tellers named is exactly what paragraph 4 calls honest; adapting a tale for children and noting the changes in a preface is acceptable, since paragraph 3 treats adapting as part of tradition and the note meets paragraph 4's honesty standard; describing her own role in shaping the record is also praised in paragraph 4. Trap: Seeing the word adapts and assuming the author objects, when the objection is to hiding it.

qs.q: Which approach is most consistent with the author’s view of oral tales?
o: An editor restores a novel to the text of the author’s original manuscript.
Not quite. This assumes an authoritative original, which paragraph 2 says oral tradition lacks.
A scholar seeks the earliest written version of a tale to identify its true form.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 rejects the idea of a pure first version.
A curator removes later additions from a medieval song collection.
Not quite. This treats later changes as contamination, the error the author identifies.
A musicologist treats each recorded performance of a traditional ballad as an equally legitimate form of the song.
Correct: this mirrors paragraph 2, where the work exists only in performances and none is privileged.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks which approach fits the author's view of oral tales. Paragraph 2 says a tale exists only in its performances, with no first telling to recover and no variant having a stronger claim than another. A musicologist who treats each recorded performance of a ballad as an equally legitimate form of the song applies that view. Why the others are wrong: restoring a novel to the author's original manuscript assumes an authoritative original, the thing paragraph 2 says oral tradition lacks; seeking the earliest written version to find a tale's true form assumes a pure first version, which paragraph 2 rejects; removing later additions from a medieval song collection treats later changes as contamination, the error the author identifies. Trap: Choosing the answer with an earlier-is-truer idea because it sounds scholarly.

passages.title: Brothers Within the Walls
text: To many economic historians, the medieval craft guild is a textbook cartel. By limiting the number of masters, fixing prices, and forbidding outsiders to sell within the town walls, guilds enriched their members at the expense of consumers and slowed innovation for centuries. The verdict has the clarity of a model, and much evidence supports it.

But the cartel story describes what guilds restricted without explaining what their members believed they were doing. Guild ordinances spend remarkable energy on matters that brought no obvious profit: the inspection of cloth for hidden flaws, the punishment of bakers who sold underweight loaves, the payment of funeral costs for poor brothers, the support of widows. A guild was also a religious brotherhood with its own altar and feast day, and in many towns a unit of the militia and a seat on the council. Membership defined a man's standing in the community, not just his trade.

Seen this way, guild rules expressed an ideal of the 'just price,' one that let an honest craftsman support his household without enriching himself at his neighbors' expense. Competition, in this moral economy, was not a neutral mechanism for discovering value but a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers. Restrictions that look like rent-seeking to a modern economist could look like integrity to a fifteenth-century weaver.

It would be sentimental to stop there. The brotherhood that supported widows also excluded Jews, foreigners, and, increasingly, women who had once practiced trades in their own right; the solidarity inside the walls was built partly on hostility toward those outside them. The point is not that guilds were benign rather than self-serving, but that the two descriptions cannot be pulled apart. Protection of members and exclusion of others were, for the guilds, the same act seen from different sides.

qs.q: According to the cartel view described in paragraph 1, guilds:
o: mainly provided welfare for widows and poor members.
Not quite. Welfare for widows comes from paragraph 2's rival view, not the cartel view in paragraph 1.
encouraged innovation by protecting skilled craftsmen from cheaper rivals in other towns.
Not quite. Paragraph 1 says guilds slowed innovation, so this says the opposite.
enriched their members by restricting competition at consumers' expense.
Correct: Paragraph 1 says guilds limited masters and fixed prices, enriching members at consumers' expense.
expressed a sincere ideal of the just price.
Not quite. The just-price ideal is paragraph 3's view, which the cartel story does not accept.
qs.x: Correct: This question points you to paragraph 1 and asks what the cartel view says. Look at the second sentence: guilds limited the number of masters, fixed prices, and kept outsiders from selling in town, and that 'enriched their members at the expense of consumers.' So the cartel view is that guilds got rich by shutting out competition and charging consumers more. Why the others are wrong: helping widows and poor members shows up in paragraph 2, as part of the author's rival moral-economy reading, not the cartel view; the cartel view says guilds slowed innovation, so 'encouraged innovation' says the opposite of paragraph 1; the sincere just-price ideal is paragraph 3's idea, which the cartel view doesn't hold. Trap: Grabbing a choice that is true somewhere in the passage but comes from a different paragraph than the one the question names.

qs.q: The author mentions cloth inspection and funeral payments primarily to:
o: show that guilds pursued aims the profit motive does not explain.
Correct: Paragraph 2 lists these as activities with 'no obvious profit,' so profit alone can't explain guilds.
prove that guilds were not cartels at all and never restricted competition.
Not quite. Too extreme. The author never denies the cartel evidence; paragraph 4 says guilds were also self-serving.
illustrate how guilds excluded outsiders.
Not quite. These examples show care for members and quality. Exclusion is paragraph 4's topic.
explain why guilds eventually disappeared.
Not quite. The passage never discusses how or why guilds disappeared.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks why the author brings up these details, so ask what job they do in the argument. They appear in paragraph 2, right after the author says the cartel story 'describes what guilds restricted without explaining what their members believed.' Cloth inspection and funeral payments are things guilds spent effort on that 'brought no obvious profit.' So they show guilds cared about aims that a pure money-making story can't explain. Why the others are wrong: saying guilds 'were not cartels at all' is too extreme, since paragraph 1 says much evidence supports the cartel verdict and paragraph 4 says guilds were also self-serving; excluding outsiders is paragraph 4's topic, and these examples are about helping members and keeping quality up; nothing in the passage discusses why guilds ended. Trap: Choosing an absolute claim like 'not cartels at all' because it sounds like the author's side, when the author only wants to add to the picture.

qs.q: In the moral economy described in paragraph 3, competition was regarded as:
o: a neutral way of discovering the value of goods in the marketplace.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says competition was 'not a neutral mechanism for discovering value.' This is what it denies.
a temptation to dishonest practices and underselling.
Correct: Paragraph 3 calls competition 'a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers.'
a religious duty owed to the brotherhood.
Not quite. Religion appears in paragraph 2, but nothing calls competition a religious duty.
the main source of the just price for goods sold in the town.
Not quite. The just price came from a moral ideal, not from competition, which paragraph 3 distrusts.
qs.x: Correct: Go to paragraph 3. It says that in this moral economy competition 'was not a neutral mechanism for discovering value but a temptation to cut corners and undersell one's brothers.' Cutting corners means dishonest work, and underselling means taking customers from fellow members. So competition was seen as a temptation to those two things. Why the others are wrong: calling it a 'neutral way of discovering value' is exactly what paragraph 3 says it was not; a religious duty to the brotherhood mixes in the guild's religious side from paragraph 2 and has nothing to do with competition; the just price came from the guild's ideal of honest living, and paragraph 3 never says competition produced it. Trap: Picking the choice that repeats the phrase from the passage even though the passage rejects it.

qs.q: What is the main function of the final paragraph?
o: To abandon the moral-economy reading in favor of the cartel model presented in paragraph 1
Not quite. The author doesn't drop the moral-economy view. Paragraph 4 says both descriptions stay together.
To argue that guilds were mainly benign institutions
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says the point is not 'benign rather than self-serving' but that both are true.
To introduce new evidence about guild pricing
Not quite. No new pricing evidence appears. The paragraph talks about who was excluded.
To argue that protection and exclusion went together
Correct: Paragraph 4 says protecting members and excluding others were 'the same act.'
qs.x: Correct: A main-function question asks what the last paragraph does for the whole argument. Paragraph 4 opens with 'It would be sentimental to stop there,' meaning don't stop at the nice moral-economy picture. It then shows the same brotherhood that helped widows shut out Jews, foreigners, and women, and ends: 'Protection of members and exclusion of others were... the same act.' So its job is to argue the two go together. Why the others are wrong: abandoning the moral-economy view is too strong, because the author keeps both views and says they 'cannot be pulled apart'; arguing guilds were 'mainly benign' goes against the author's own line that the point is not benign versus self-serving; no new pricing evidence appears in paragraph 4, which talks about who was excluded. Trap: Reading the warning against sentimentality as a full switch back to the cartel view.

qs.q: Which modern institution most closely resembles the guild as the author portrays it?
o: A licensing board that enforces ethical standards and also limits entry into a profession
Correct: It enforces standards (like guild inspections) and limits entry (like guild restrictions), matching both halves.
An open online community that anyone may join and leave freely without paying fees or meeting standards
Not quite. Open to everyone with no standards matches neither the standards nor the exclusion.
A commodity exchange where prices are set purely by bidding
Not quite. Pure bidding is the neutral competition that paragraph 3 says guilds distrusted.
A charity that gives aid to anyone in need without asking them to meet any standard or join any group
Not quite. Aid to anyone, with no conditions, lacks the exclusion that paragraph 4 treats as part of the guild.
qs.x: Correct: This asks you to match the author's picture of the guild to something modern. The author's guild does two things at once: it enforces standards and cares for members (paragraph 2: cloth inspection, honest weights) and it limits who gets in (paragraphs 1 and 4). A licensing board that sets ethical standards and also limits entry into a profession does both. Why the others are wrong: an open online community anyone can join with no standards has neither the standards nor the limited entry; a commodity exchange with prices set purely by bidding is the 'neutral mechanism' of competition that paragraph 3 says guilds distrusted; a charity helping anyone without conditions has the care but not the membership limits or the standards. Trap: Picking the choice that matches only half of the portrait, such as the caring half, when the author insists the two halves cannot be separated.

qs.q: Suppose records showed that a guild loosened its quality inspections whenever it could raise prices without penalty. This would most weaken the claim that:
o: guilds limited the number of masters.
Not quite. Loosened inspections for profit would, if anything, fit the cartel claim that guilds limited masters.
guilds excluded Jews, foreigners and women from becoming masters in the trade.
Not quite. Paragraph 4's exclusion is a separate fact. Inspection records don't touch it.
guild rules reflected members' sincere commitment to honest work.
Correct: Cutting inspections when prices could rise suggests profit, not sincere commitment to honest work.
guilds served religious and civic roles.
Not quite. Religious and civic roles from paragraph 2 are unrelated to pricing and inspection records.
qs.x: Correct: A 'weaken' question asks which claim the new fact hurts. The new fact says a guild relaxed quality inspections whenever it could raise prices safely. That suggests inspections were about profit, not about caring for honest work. The claim about 'sincere commitment to honest work' comes from paragraphs 2 and 3, where inspection of cloth and punishing short-weight bakers show integrity. So it is hit hardest. Why the others are wrong: limiting the number of masters is part of the cartel view, and this finding would actually support it; excluding Jews, foreigners, and women is a separate fact from paragraph 4 and says nothing about inspections; the religious and civic roles from paragraph 2 are not touched by pricing and inspection records. Trap: Choosing a claim the new fact is merely near, instead of the one it actually contradicts.

passages.title: Words at Work
text: For much of the history of philosophy, the meaning of a word was thought to be the thing it stood for. 'Apple' meant apples; 'justice' meant some more elusive object that philosophers were charged with locating. The later Wittgenstein proposed a different picture. Words, he suggested, are less like labels than like tools, and their meanings are found in the uses to which they are put within particular activities, which he called language-games. A builder who calls out 'Slab!' to an assistant is not naming an object for contemplation but giving an instruction within a shared task.

Critics have often heard this as a recipe for relativism. If meaning is simply use, and different communities use words differently, then it seems no use can be wrong and no claim can be criticized from outside its own game. This reading, though common, misunderstands the analogy. Games have rules, and a move can be mistaken: one can castle illegally in chess or call a strike when the pitch was wide. To say that meaning lies in use is to say that it lies in a practice with standards of correctness, not in whatever a speaker happens to intend.

The more interesting consequence of the view is not relativism but a diagnosis of confusion. Many apparent disagreements arise when a word migrates from one game to another while carrying the expectations of its first home. When an economist and a theologian argue about whether a gift can ever be truly 'free,' they may not be disputing a fact at all, but talking past each other with a single word that does different work in each of their practices.

The lesson is not that every dispute dissolves under analysis. Some disagreements are genuine and must be argued out. But before we argue, it is worth asking whether we are playing the same game, and whether the word at the center of the quarrel means for our opponent what it means for us.

qs.q: According to the passage, the traditional view held that a word's meaning is:
o: the use it is put to within an activity.
Not quite. Meaning as use is the later Wittgenstein's new proposal, not the traditional view.
whatever the speaker happens to intend.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 rejects this idea. It is not called the traditional view.
a rule within a shared game.
Not quite. Rules of a game belong to the newer language-game picture.
the thing the word stands for.
Correct: Paragraph 1 says the traditional view was that meaning is the thing the word stands for.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks about the 'traditional view,' so look for where the author describes older thinking. Paragraph 1 starts: 'For much of the history of philosophy, the meaning of a word was thought to be the thing it stood for.' The example is that 'Apple' meant apples. Why the others are wrong: meaning as the use within an activity is the later Wittgenstein's new view, not the traditional one; paragraph 2 rejects meaning as 'whatever a speaker happens to intend,' and doesn't call it traditional; a rule within a shared game is also part of the newer picture, in paragraphs 1 and 2. Trap: Choosing the answer that is the passage's main idea instead of the older idea the question asks about.

qs.q: The examples of illegal castling and a mistaken strike call are offered to show that:
o: games are a poor analogy for language because games have written rules.
Not quite. The author defends the game analogy. Nothing says it fails for lack of written rules.
meaning grounded in use still allows for mistakes.
Correct: Illegal castling and a wrongly called strike show that a move can be mistaken even when meaning comes from use.
different communities play the same games differently and follow different rules.
Not quite. That is the critics' worry in paragraph 2, not what the examples are meant to show.
umpires and referees decide what words mean.
Not quite. The umpire is just part of the baseball example. Nobody says umpires decide word meanings.
qs.x: Correct: Ask why the author uses chess and baseball. They show up in paragraph 2, right after critics say that if meaning is use, 'no use can be wrong.' The author replies that games have rules and a move can be mistaken: castling illegally in chess, calling a strike on a wide pitch. So meaning based on use still has right and wrong. Why the others are wrong: the author uses games as a good analogy and never says written rules are a problem; the claim that communities play games differently is the critics' worry, not what the examples are meant to show; umpires appear only inside the baseball example and nobody says they decide word meanings. Trap: Picking a choice that sounds like the critics' side, which is the view the author is answering.

qs.q: The author's reply to the charge of relativism would be most weakened if it were shown that:
o: many disputes arise when words move between practices that use them in different ways.
Not quite. Words migrating between games is the author's own point in paragraph 3 and doesn't hurt the reply.
some disagreements are genuine and must be argued out.
Not quite. Genuine disagreements fit with standards of correctness. They don't undermine the reply.
language-games lack any shared standards by which a move can be judged wrong.
Correct: If no shared standards exist to call a move wrong, the author's rule-based answer to relativism fails.
builders rarely shout single-word commands.
Not quite. This only touches the builder example in paragraph 1, not the reply to relativism.
qs.x: Correct: The author's reply to the relativism charge is in paragraph 2: games have rules, so a practice has 'standards of correctness.' To weaken that reply, find a fact that says those standards don't exist. If language-games lacked any shared standards for judging a move wrong, the reply would fall apart, and the critics would be right. Why the others are wrong: words moving between practices is the paragraph 3 point, which the author already accepts and which doesn't touch the standards claim; genuine disagreements needing argument is from paragraph 4 and is consistent with standards; builders rarely shouting commands only affects an example in paragraph 1. Trap: Choosing a claim that attacks something in the passage, but not the particular argument the question names.

qs.q: Which scenario best illustrates the kind of confusion described in paragraph 3?
o: A doctor and patient read 'chronic' differently
Correct: One word, 'chronic,' does different work for doctor and patient, so they talk past each other.
Two chess players disagree about whether a particular move broke the rules of the game they agreed on
Not quite. These players share the game and its rules. That is a genuine disagreement, not a word migrating.
Two historians disagree about the date of a battle
Not quite. Two historians dispute a fact. Paragraph 3's confusion is not about a fact.
A child learns the word 'apple' by being shown an apple
Not quite. Learning a word from its object is the traditional picture in paragraph 1, not a confusion.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 describes confusion that arises when 'a word migrates from one game to another while carrying the expectations of its first home,' like economist and theologian talking past each other about 'free.' A doctor and patient reading 'chronic' differently fits: one word, two practices, two meanings, so they talk past each other. Why the others are wrong: two chess players disputing whether a move broke the rules share the same game and the same meaning, which is a genuine disagreement; two historians arguing over a battle date are disputing a fact, which paragraph 3 says is not the case in this confusion; a child learning 'apple' from an apple is the traditional picture from paragraph 1, not a confusion. Trap: Picking any example that involves two people disagreeing.

qs.q: What does the author ultimately recommend?
o: Treat every disagreement as a misunderstanding about the meanings of the words involved.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says some disagreements are genuine, so this is too extreme.
Before arguing, check whether both sides use the key word the same way.
Correct: Paragraph 4 advises asking whether both sides mean the same thing by the central word before arguing.
Return to defining words by the objects they name.
Not quite. Defining words by the objects they name is the old view the author moves away from.
Avoid disputes between different academic fields.
Not quite. The author never says to avoid disputes. The advice is to check the word's use first.
qs.x: Correct: 'Ultimately recommends' points to the end. Paragraph 4 says: 'before we argue, it is worth asking whether we are playing the same game, and whether the word at the center of the quarrel means for our opponent what it means for us.' So check whether both sides use the key word the same way. Why the others are wrong: treating every disagreement as a misunderstanding goes against paragraph 4, which says the lesson is not that 'every dispute dissolves under analysis' because some are genuine; returning to meaning as named objects is the traditional view the author moves away from; avoiding disputes between fields is never suggested, since the economist and theologian example is about checking, not avoiding. Trap: Choosing the extreme version (every dispute) of a point the author makes only in moderate form.

passages.title: The Instructed Child
text: Histories of children's literature tend to follow a plot of liberation. In the beginning, we are told, were the improving tracts of the eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, in which disobedient children fell into ponds and pious ones died serenely, and in which every story ended in a lesson. Then came Lewis Carroll, whose Alice tumbled into a world of nonsense where the morals were mocked, and children's books were set free to delight rather than instruct.

The plot has its truth. Carroll did parody the moral verses that Victorian children memorized, and the books that followed him gave imagination a standing it had seldom enjoyed. But the liberation narrative mistakes a change in what children's books teach for a change in whether they teach. Walk through the picture-book section of any modern bookstore and you will find books about sharing, about naming one's feelings, about welcoming the new child in class, about the dignity of every kind of family. These books are no less earnest than the tracts they supposedly replaced. They have simply exchanged obedience and piety for empathy and self-acceptance.

This is not a complaint. Adults who write for children are, almost unavoidably, telling them what kind of people to become, and it would be strange to wish otherwise. The trouble with the liberation story is that it lets each generation imagine that its own lessons are not lessons at all but simply the truth, while the moralizing belongs only to the past. The Victorian author who warned against vanity believed he was describing reality, not imposing a value. So, very often, do we.

A more honest history would read the didactic tract and the contemporary picture book side by side, as documents of what different societies hoped their children would be. It would also ask why the books children love most, from Carroll's to the present, so often seem to slip free of whatever lesson the adults intended.

qs.q: The author's main objection to the liberation narrative is that it:
o: exaggerates the harshness of early moral tracts.
Not quite. The author doesn't argue about how harsh the tracts were.
gives Lewis Carroll too little credit.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the plot 'has its truth' about Carroll.
mistakes a change in what children's books teach for an end to teaching.
Correct: Paragraph 2 says the narrative confuses a change in what books teach with a change in whether they teach.
ignores the commercial pressures that shaped what publishers would print for children.
Not quite. Publishers and commercial pressure never come up.
qs.x: Correct: The author's objection is in paragraph 2: 'the liberation narrative mistakes a change in what children's books teach for a change in whether they teach.' Modern picture books about sharing and feelings are 'no less earnest' than the old tracts. So it mistakes a change in lessons for an end to teaching. Why the others are wrong: exaggerating the harshness of the tracts isn't the complaint, and the author doesn't defend them either; giving Carroll too little credit is wrong because paragraph 2 says Carroll did parody moral verses and gave imagination standing; commercial pressures on publishers are never mentioned. Trap: Choosing a criticism that sounds like a typical complaint about a history, not the one this author makes.

qs.q: The author's remark about the Victorian author who warned against vanity, followed by 'So, very often, do we,' suggests that:
o: modern writers also tend to mistake their own values for plain truth.
Correct: The Victorian believed he described reality, 'so, very often, do we,' meaning modern writers do too.
modern writers warn against vanity more often and more forcefully than Victorian writers did.
Not quite. Vanity was only an example. Nothing compares modern and Victorian forcefulness.
Victorian authors knowingly imposed their values.
Not quite. The passage says the Victorian author believed he was describing reality, not imposing a value.
readers today reject moral lessons in children's books.
Not quite. The author argues modern books still teach, so readers haven't rejected lessons.
qs.x: Correct: The sentence is in paragraph 3: the Victorian author who warned against vanity 'believed he was describing reality, not imposing a value. So, very often, do we.' 'We' means modern writers, so the line suggests modern writers also mistake their own values for plain truth. Why the others are wrong: warning against vanity more forcefully than the Victorians is never said, since vanity was only an example; Victorian authors knowingly imposing values contradicts the sentence, which says he believed he was just describing reality; readers today rejecting moral lessons is the liberation story the author challenges. Trap: Taking an example (vanity) as the topic instead of the point it illustrates.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward instruction in children's books is best described as:
o: disapproving, since lessons stifle children's imagination and their pleasure in reading.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 says 'This is not a complaint,' so it isn't disapproval.
nostalgic for the moral clarity of the earlier tracts and their direct lessons.
Not quite. The author never longs for the earlier tracts.
indifferent, since children ignore lessons anyway.
Not quite. The author clearly cares, since the passage argues for a more honest history.
accepting of it as nearly unavoidable while urging awareness of it.
Correct: The author calls teaching almost unavoidable and urges honesty about it.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 says 'This is not a complaint. Adults who write for children are, almost unavoidably, telling them what kind of people to become.' But the author also wants writers to realize they're doing it, and paragraph 4 calls for a more honest history. That is accepting instruction as nearly unavoidable while urging awareness. Why the others are wrong: disapproving contradicts 'this is not a complaint'; nostalgic for the older tracts isn't stated; indifferent is wrong because the author cares enough to correct the narrative. Trap: Choosing a tone word from only one sentence, rather than the whole passage.

qs.q: Which research project would the author most likely recommend?
o: Measuring whether modern picture books raise children's empathy scores more than Victorian tracts did
Not quite. The author doesn't suggest measuring effects on children.
Comparing a Victorian moral tract with a recent picture book as evidence of each era's ideals
Correct: Paragraph 4 recommends reading a tract and a modern picture book side by side as documents of each era's hopes.
Cataloging which moral verses Carroll parodied in his books
Not quite. Cataloging Carroll's parodies is a narrow detail, not the author's proposal.
Surveying parents on which lessons they want books to teach
Not quite. Parent surveys don't read the books side by side.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 proposes the author's project: 'A more honest history would read the didactic tract and the contemporary picture book side by side, as documents of what different societies hoped their children would be.' Comparing a Victorian tract with a recent picture book as evidence of each era's ideals matches. Why the others are wrong: measuring whether modern books raise empathy scores more than Victorian ones is about effects, and the author never discusses measuring them; cataloging the verses Carroll parodied is a narrow detail from paragraph 2; surveying parents about preferred lessons isn't about what the books say. Trap: Picking a project that sounds scholarly but isn't the one the passage describes.

qs.q: The final sentence of the passage most strongly implies that the books children love most:
o: contain no moral content at all.
Not quite. Slipping free of the intended lesson is not the same as having no moral content.
were written without any adult intention.
Not quite. The sentence assumes adults did intend a lesson.
owe part of their appeal to what escapes their authors' intended lessons.
Correct: Books that slip free of intended lessons owe part of their appeal to what escapes them.
are mostly nonsense books written in Carroll's tradition of parody.
Not quite. Carroll is one example. The sentence doesn't say these books are mostly nonsense.
qs.x: Correct: The last sentence asks why the books children love most 'so often seem to slip free of whatever lesson the adults intended.' That implies part of their appeal comes from what escapes the authors' lessons. Why the others are wrong: 'no moral content at all' is too extreme, since the sentence says they slip free of the intended lesson, not that there is none; being written without adult intention contradicts 'the lesson the adults intended'; being mostly nonsense in Carroll's tradition is an overreach, since Carroll appears as one example among books children love. Trap: Taking 'slip free of' to mean 'have none.'

passages.title: Stories Told From the Center
text: Every society that has pushed against an edge has told stories about the edge. In the United States the most famous version was given scholarly form in 1893, when a young historian argued that the availability of open land had shaped the national character, producing individualism, practical ingenuity and a democratic suspicion of inherited rank. The thesis was elegant, and it arrived just as the census office had announced that a continuous line of settlement could no longer be drawn on the map.

That timing deserves more attention than the thesis itself. A myth of the frontier is rarely composed on the frontier. It is composed afterward, in cities, by people who feel the loss of something they never personally possessed. The settlers whose diaries survive wrote mostly about debt, weather, illness and the price of seed. The grand narrative of self-reliance belongs to their grandchildren, who needed an origin story capable of reassuring an industrial and increasingly crowded nation that its virtues had been forged somewhere wider than a factory floor.

Read this way, frontier myths are documents of the center rather than of the margin. They record what a settled society fears it lacks. Where the city feels hemmed in, the myth supplies space; where the corporation dissolves individual achievement, the myth supplies the lone homesteader; where politics feels corrupt, the myth supplies a simpler justice. The people already living on the supposedly open land appear in such stories chiefly as obstacles or as scenery, a revealing absence that tells us whose needs the story serves.

None of this means the myths are merely false. They have real effects, shaping policy, advertising and the private ambitions of people who will never see a prairie. But their truth is the truth of a symptom. To ask whether the frontier really produced self-reliant democrats is to ask the wrong question. The better question is why a nation, at a particular moment, needed so badly to believe that it had.

qs.q: The author's main point is that frontier myths are best understood as:
o: evidence about the anxieties of the settled society that tells them.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says myths are documents of the center that record what a settled society fears it lacks.
accurate accounts of how open land shaped national character.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 calls the question of whether the frontier really produced these virtues the wrong question.
harmless fictions with little effect on public life.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says the myths have real effects on policy and ambitions.
records written by settlers about their daily hardships.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the myth was composed afterward by the settlers' grandchildren, not by the settlers.
qs.x: Correct: The main point comes together in paragraph 3 and 4. Paragraph 3 says 'frontier myths are documents of the center rather than of the margin. They record what a settled society fears it lacks.' So they are best understood as evidence about the anxieties of the society that tells them. Why the others are wrong: accurate accounts of how open land shaped character is the thesis the author sets aside in paragraph 4 ('the wrong question'); harmless fictions with little effect is denied in paragraph 4, which says myths shape policy, advertising and ambitions; records written by settlers is wrong because paragraph 2 says the myth was composed later by their grandchildren. Trap: Choosing a choice that mixes up who wrote the myth and who the myth is about.

qs.q: The author mentions settlers' diaries about debt, weather and seed prices primarily in order to:
o: show that settlers were more self-reliant than historians believed.
Not quite. The diaries show ordinary worries, not extra self-reliance.
argue that diaries are the most reliable historical sources.
Not quite. The author doesn't rank sources by reliability.
contrast settlers' actual concerns with the later myth of self-reliance.
Correct: Diaries about debt and seed prices contrast with the later grand narrative of self-reliance.
explain why the frontier thesis appeared in 1893.
Not quite. The timing point comes from the census announcement in paragraph 1.
qs.x: Correct: The diaries are in paragraph 2: settlers wrote 'mostly about debt, weather, illness and the price of seed.' The next sentence says 'The grand narrative of self-reliance belongs to their grandchildren.' So the diaries contrast what settlers actually worried about with the later myth. Why the others are wrong: showing settlers were more self-reliant than historians believed is the opposite; arguing diaries are the most reliable sources makes a general claim the author doesn't make; explaining why the thesis appeared in 1893 comes from the census point in paragraph 1, not from the diaries. Trap: Choosing a reason that sounds like what historians do with diaries.

qs.q: According to paragraph 3, people already living on the 'supposedly open land' appear in frontier myths mainly as:
o: heroic models of self-reliance.
Not quite. The homesteader is the hero. The people already living there are not.
the main authors of the stories.
Not quite. The myths are composed at the center, not by those living on the land.
obstacles or scenery.
Correct: Paragraph 3 says they appear 'chiefly as obstacles or as scenery.'
victims whose losses the myths mourn.
Not quite. The myths don't mourn their losses. They mostly leave them out.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 ends: 'The people already living on the supposedly open land appear in such stories chiefly as obstacles or as scenery, a revealing absence.' Why the others are wrong: heroic models of self-reliance misses that the lone homesteader is the hero; being the main authors is wrong since the stories come from the center; victims whose losses the myths mourn is wrong because the stories treat them as obstacles or scenery, not as mourned. Trap: Choosing a sympathetic reading the passage doesn't give.

qs.q: In saying that the myths possess 'the truth of a symptom,' the author most likely means that they:
o: reveal real underlying needs even when they misdescribe the past.
Correct: Like a symptom, a myth reveals real needs of the society, even if it misdescribes the past.
are true only for the generation that first experienced the frontier.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the settlers' own concerns were different from the myth.
describe a disease that weakened the national character.
Not quite. 'Symptom' is a metaphor, and the passage doesn't mention a disease.
were proven accurate in most details by later historical research.
Not quite. The author says whether the frontier produced these virtues is the wrong question.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 4 says myths 'have real effects... But their truth is the truth of a symptom.' A symptom shows something about the body even if it doesn't describe the cause correctly. So myths reveal real underlying needs even when they misdescribe the past. Why the others are wrong: true only for the first generation contradicts paragraph 2, which says the settlers' own concerns were different; describing a disease that weakened the national character takes 'symptom' literally; being proven accurate by research goes against paragraph 4's 'wrong question.' Trap: Taking a metaphor literally.

qs.q: Which finding would most strengthen the author's argument?
