o: Most frontier novels were written by people who had lived on homesteads and farmed the land themselves.
Not quite. Homesteader authors would weaken the claim that the myths come from the center.
Frontier novels sold best in cities during corporate booms.
Correct: City readers buying frontier stories during corporate booms fits myths answering what the center feels it lacks.
Settlers' diaries frequently praised individualism and self-reliance.
Not quite. Diaries praising self-reliance would weaken the contrast the author draws in paragraph 2.
Frontier myths had little influence on later government land policy.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says myths do shape policy, so this would weaken the argument.
qs.x: Correct: The author's argument is that frontier myths are composed in cities by people who feel a loss and need a story (paragraphs 2 and 3). Frontier novels selling best in cities during corporate booms fits: the myth's supply of lone achievement was in demand when corporations dissolved individual achievement. Why the others are wrong: novels written by people who farmed homesteads would weaken the idea that myths come from the center; diaries often praising self-reliance would weaken the contrast in paragraph 2; myths having little influence on policy conflicts with paragraph 4. Trap: Choosing a finding that sounds historical but doesn't touch the center-versus-margin claim.

qs.q: Which situation is most analogous to the author's account of frontier myths?
o: Farmers keep careful ledgers of rainfall and crop prices each season.
Not quite. Ledgers are practical records, not a story that fills a felt lack.
A historian corrects errors in an earlier account of a famous battle using newly discovered letters from soldiers.
Not quite. Correcting errors with evidence is the kind of question the author sets aside.
A village records its own festivals in a locally kept chronicle that is read aloud each year.
Not quite. A village telling its own story is a story from the margin, not from the center.
Films romanticizing village life thrive in fast-growing cities during housing shortages.
Correct: Crowded city dwellers consume romantic village films, just as the center wanted space and a simpler life from the frontier myth.
qs.x: Correct: The author says myths come from the center and supply what a settled society feels it lacks (paragraph 3). Films romanticizing village life thriving in fast-growing cities during housing shortages fits: a crowded city imagines a simpler place. Why the others are wrong: farmers keeping careful ledgers is practical record keeping; a historian correcting a battle account with newly found letters is a correction by evidence, which is the opposite of the myth's symptom role; a village recording its own festivals is a story from the margin about itself, not from the center. Trap: Choosing an example that involves stories or records without asking who tells them and why.

passages.title: The Retreating Mirage
text: Few complaints are as common among travelers as the complaint that a place has been ruined by tourists. The village festival has become a show, the market sells souvenirs made elsewhere, the dancers perform on a schedule printed in the hotel lobby. The traveler who voices this complaint usually exempts himself from the crowd he blames, imagining that he alone came looking for the real thing.

Sociologists have long described the resulting predicament. Hosts, aware that visitors crave authenticity, stage a version of it, arranging back regions that appear private but are designed to be seen. Visitors, sensing the staging, push further in search of something unarranged, and the hosts follow. On this view, authenticity is a mirage that retreats as the tourist approaches, and every encounter is quietly counterfeit.

The analysis is shrewd, but it smuggles in an assumption I find untenable: that a practice performed for outsiders is thereby less genuine than one performed for insiders alone. Cultures have always presented themselves to visitors, and the presentation is itself a cultural act. A dance revived for tourist audiences may be learned by young people who would otherwise have let it lapse, debated by elders over what counts as correct, and altered in ways the community chooses. To call the result fake is to deny the community the right that every culture exercises, the right to change.

The deeper problem lies in the tourist's ideal. The longing for the untouched place casts its residents as inhabitants of the past, people whose value depends on their remaining unlike the visitor. Smartphones in the market, a pop song from a doorway, a guide who studied business administration: these register as intrusions only because the traveler has decided in advance what the place is for. Authenticity, if the word is worth keeping, should describe the relation between a people and their practices, not the match between a destination and a visitor's expectations.

qs.q: Which statement best captures the author's position?
o: Practices performed for tourists can be authentic; the trouble lies in what tourists expect.
Correct: Paragraphs 3 and 4 say performing for tourists isn't fake and the problem is the tourists' expectations.
Tourism inevitably makes every cultural encounter counterfeit.
Not quite. That is the sociologists' mirage view, which the author rejects.
Authenticity can be found only in places that tourists have not yet reached or changed.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 criticizes the longing for the untouched place.
Communities should stop performing traditional dances for visitors.
Not quite. The author defends performances for visitors and doesn't call for them to stop.
qs.x: Correct: The author's position is clearest in paragraph 3 ('a practice performed for outsiders' isn't less genuine) and paragraph 4: authenticity 'should describe the relation between a people and their practices, not the match between a destination and a visitor's expectations.' So practices for tourists can be authentic, and the trouble is what tourists expect. Why the others are wrong: tourism making every encounter counterfeit is the sociologists' view that the author rejects; authenticity found only in untouched places is the tourist's ideal criticized in paragraph 4; stopping dances for visitors is not recommended. Trap: Choosing a view the author argues against.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the sociological analysis in paragraph 2 is best described as:
o: wholly dismissive of its account of staged authenticity and back regions.
Not quite. The author calls the analysis shrewd, so it isn't wholly dismissive.
fully supportive, since it explains why places are ruined by visitors.
Not quite. The author finds one assumption untenable, so support isn't full.
indifferent, since it concerns hosts rather than tourists.
Not quite. The author engages with it at length.
appreciative of its insight but critical of a hidden assumption.
Correct: Paragraph 3 calls it shrewd but says it smuggles in an untenable assumption.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3 begins: 'The analysis is shrewd, but it smuggles in an assumption I find untenable.' Shrewd is praise; untenable is criticism of the hidden assumption. So the attitude is appreciative of its insight but critical of a hidden assumption. Why the others are wrong: wholly dismissive ignores 'shrewd'; fully supportive ignores 'untenable'; indifferent is wrong because the author spends a whole paragraph on it. Trap: Choosing an all-or-nothing attitude when the author is mixed.

qs.q: The example of a dance revived for tourist audiences is used to show that:
o: tourist demand always distorts traditional forms beyond recognition, whatever the community intends.
Not quite. The author uses the example to argue against distortion being inevitable.
elders oppose any change to traditional practices.
Not quite. The elders debate what is correct, which isn't opposing all change.
performing for outsiders can involve real community choice and continuity.
Correct: Young people learn it, elders debate it, and the community alters it as it chooses.
dances are the only practices tourists find authentic.
Not quite. The passage doesn't say dances are the only practices tourists find authentic.
qs.x: Correct: The dance example is in paragraph 3: a dance revived for tourist audiences 'may be learned by young people who would otherwise have let it lapse, debated by elders over what counts as correct, and altered in ways the community chooses.' So performing for outsiders can involve real community choice and continuity. Why the others are wrong: tourist demand always distorting traditions is the view the author rejects; elders opposing all change contradicts the elders debating correctness; dances being the only practices tourists find authentic isn't claimed. Trap: Choosing the pessimistic view the example is answering.

qs.q: In noting that the complaining traveler 'exempts himself from the crowd he blames,' the author implies that:
o: solitary travelers are more respectful than tour groups.
Not quite. The passage doesn't compare solitary travelers and tour groups.
the complainer shares the very tourist position he criticizes.
Correct: By exempting himself, the complainer overlooks that he is one of the tourists.
complaints about tourism are usually accurate.
Not quite. The author is skeptical of the complaint, not endorsing it.
locals blame individual travelers for overcrowding.
Not quite. What locals think isn't discussed.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 1 says the traveler 'usually exempts himself from the crowd he blames, imagining that he alone came looking for the real thing.' The author's point is that he is himself a tourist, so he shares the very position he criticizes. Why the others are wrong: solitary travelers being more respectful isn't claimed; complaints being usually accurate is the opposite of the author's skepticism; locals blaming individual travelers for overcrowding isn't mentioned. Trap: Picking a generalization the sentence doesn't support.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the argument in paragraph 3?
o: Young residents often learn revived dances to perform them for visitors.
Not quite. This supports the author's point about revival.
Tourist dances are typically choreographed by outside tour firms, excluding residents.
Correct: Outside choreography with residents excluded removes the community choice that paragraph 3 relies on.
Some tourists prefer performances they believe are unstaged.
Not quite. Tourist preferences don't affect whether the community chooses.
Residents of tourist towns frequently own smartphones.
Not quite. Smartphones relate to paragraph 4, not the argument in paragraph 3.
qs.x: Correct: Paragraph 3's argument is that a practice performed for outsiders can still be a genuine cultural act and the community's own choice. If tourist dances are typically choreographed by outside tour firms, excluding residents, the community isn't choosing, and the argument weakens. Why the others are wrong: young residents learning revived dances supports the argument; some tourists preferring unstaged shows is about tourists, not about the community's role; residents owning smartphones is from paragraph 4's ideal, not paragraph 3's argument. Trap: Choosing a fact that touches the topic but not the claim in the paragraph named.

passages.title: Legible Hands
text: Every restoration of an old painting rests on an answer, usually unspoken, to a deceptively simple question: what is the painting? For much of the nineteenth century the answer was the image the artist intended, and restorers acted accordingly, repainting lost passages, scrubbing away darkened varnish, and occasionally 'improving' a composition they judged clumsy. The results were often handsome and nearly always irreversible. A restorer confident that he knew what the master meant had no reason to leave a trace of himself.

The reaction against this confidence produced its own orthodoxy. Critics began to celebrate patina, the yellowed varnish and fine cracking that time lays over a canvas, as an integral part of the work. To clean a painting, on this view, was to erase its biography. But the cult of patina is no more modest than the cult of intention; it merely transfers authority from the artist to the centuries, and it can license neglect as easily as the older view licensed overpainting. A varnish so dark that the figures beneath it are illegible does not preserve a history. It conceals one.

I would propose a different answer. A painting is both an image and a document, and restoration ought to respect the second role without abandoning the first. This is the logic behind the Italian practice of tratteggio, in which losses are filled with fine vertical hatching that blends into the surrounding paint at a normal viewing distance but reveals itself on close inspection. The viewer sees a coherent picture; the scholar sees exactly where the original stops.

The principle can be stated simply: an intervention should be legible and, wherever possible, reversible. Legibility admits that the restorer is a later hand, working with later knowledge and later taste. Reversibility admits that this knowledge will itself be superseded. Neither principle tells us how far to clean a particular picture, and honest conservators will continue to disagree about that. What the principles rule out is the pretense that any restoration can be invisible, as though the painting had simply been returned to a moment that, in truth, no one alive has ever seen.

qs.q: According to the passage, tratteggio is valuable because it:
o: restores a painting exactly to the artist's original intention
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says no restoration can be invisible or return a painting to the original moment.
preserves the darkened varnish that records a painting's age
Not quite. Preserving varnish is the patina view, a different approach.
allows restorers to correct compositional flaws in the original
Not quite. Correcting flaws is the nineteenth-century habit the author criticizes.
blends in at viewing distance yet shows its boundaries up close
Correct: Tratteggio blends in at normal viewing distance but reveals itself on close inspection.
qs.x: Correct: This asks why the passage values tratteggio. Paragraph 3 describes it as filling losses "with fine vertical hatching that blends into the surrounding paint at a normal viewing distance but reveals itself on close inspection." So it blends in at a distance yet shows its boundaries up close. Why the others are wrong: restoring the artist's exact intention is the nineteenth-century goal the author criticizes; preserving darkened varnish is the patina view of paragraph 2; correcting compositional flaws is the "improving" of paragraph 1. Trap: Picking a restoration goal the passage mentions but doesn't link to tratteggio.

qs.q: The author's main objection to the 'cult of patina' is that it:
o: hands authority to time and can excuse neglect
Correct: Paragraph 2 says it transfers authority to the centuries and can license neglect.
encourages restorers to repaint lost passages of the original in their own style
Not quite. Repainting is the fault of the older view in paragraph 1.
relies on chemical methods that damage the canvas
Not quite. Chemical methods are never mentioned.
treats the painting as a document rather than an image
Not quite. The author wants the painting treated as both a document and an image.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks for the author's main objection to the cult of patina. Paragraph 2 says it "merely transfers authority from the artist to the centuries, and it can license neglect as easily as the older view licensed overpainting." So it hands authority to time and can excuse neglect. Why the others are wrong: repainting in the restorer's own style describes the older intention view in paragraph 1; relying on chemical methods that damage the canvas is never mentioned; treating the painting as a document rather than an image isn't the objection, since the author wants both roles respected. Trap: Attaching the older view's fault to the newer one.

qs.q: The final phrase, 'a moment that, in truth, no one alive has ever seen,' suggests that:
o: old paintings were rarely displayed when they were first made
Not quite. The phrase doesn't concern how often paintings were displayed.
restorers should consult eyewitness accounts of original works before cleaning them
Not quite. No one alive could have seen the original moment, and the passage doesn't suggest consulting accounts.
a painting's original appearance is not directly known to anyone today
Correct: No one alive has seen the original moment, so a painting's original look isn't directly known.
modern viewers lack the taste to appreciate old paintings
Not quite. The passage says nothing about modern taste in this sentence.
qs.x: Correct: This asks what "a moment that, in truth, no one alive has ever seen" suggests. Paragraph 4 says the pretense that restoration can be invisible assumes the painting can be "returned to a moment" that no one alive has seen. So the painting's original appearance isn't directly known to anyone today. Why the others are wrong: old paintings being rarely displayed is never said; consulting eyewitness accounts is not advised, and no living person could be an eyewitness; modern viewers lacking taste isn't the point. Trap: Reading a literal historical claim into a rhetorical phrase.

qs.q: The author's call for reversible restoration depends most on which assumption?
o: Original paint is always more valuable than restorers' additions.
Not quite. The reasoning is about future knowledge, not the value of paint.
Later conservators may know things that make present choices look wrong.
Correct: Reversibility admits that present knowledge will be superseded by later knowledge.
Most viewers can easily tell restored passages from the original paint around them.
Not quite. Tratteggio is meant to blend at a distance, so easy detection isn't assumed.
Patina is the most important record of a painting's history and must never be removed.
Not quite. The author criticizes treating patina as untouchable.
qs.x: Correct: This asks what the call for reversibility depends on. Paragraph 4 says "Reversibility admits that this knowledge will itself be superseded." So it assumes later conservators may know things that make present choices look wrong. Why the others are wrong: original paint always being more valuable isn't the reason given; viewers easily telling restored from original is not assumed, since tratteggio is designed to blend at a distance; patina being most important and never removed is the cult the author criticizes. Trap: Choosing an assumption that sounds protective of the original instead of the humility the author states.

qs.q: A museum repaints a damaged face so seamlessly that experts cannot find the repair even under magnification, but uses a paint that can be fully removed. The author would most likely:
o: praise the repair because it restores the artist's intended image
Not quite. Restoring the artist's intended image is the older view the author criticizes.
reject the repair because any filling of losses is improper
Not quite. The author supports filling losses legibly, as with tratteggio.
accept the repair fully, since it can be undone later
Not quite. Reversibility is only one of two principles; legibility is also required.
approve its reversibility but object to its look
Correct: The paint is reversible, but an invisible repair is not legible, which breaks the second principle.
qs.x: Correct: This asks how the author would react to an invisible, fully removable repaint. Paragraph 4 says an intervention should be "legible and, wherever possible, reversible" and rejects "the pretense that any restoration can be invisible." The paint is reversible, which the author wants, but experts can't find the repair even under magnification, so it isn't legible. Why the others are wrong: praising it for restoring the intended image is the nineteenth-century view; rejecting any filling is too strong, since tratteggio fills losses; accepting it fully because it can be undone ignores the legibility requirement. Trap: Treating one of two requirements as enough.

qs.q: Which discovery would most strengthen the author's criticism of nineteenth-century restoration?
o: A famous 'improvement' rested on a misreading, but cannot be removed without harm.
Correct: A mistaken improvement that can't be undone shows the danger of confident, irreversible restoration.
Some nineteenth-century restorers kept detailed records of their work, including what they repainted.
Not quite. Detailed records would soften the criticism of leaving no trace.
Darkened varnish slowly damages the paint layer beneath it.
Not quite. This targets the patina view, not nineteenth-century restoration.
Modern viewers prefer cleaned paintings to uncleaned ones when shown both side by side.
Not quite. Viewer preferences today don't test the criticism of earlier methods.
qs.x: Correct: This asks what would most strengthen the author's criticism of nineteenth-century restoration. Paragraph 1 faults it as confident, trace-free and "nearly always irreversible." A famous "improvement" that rested on a misreading and can't be removed without harm shows exactly the danger of confidence plus irreversibility. Why the others are wrong: detailed records kept by restorers would soften the criticism; darkened varnish damaging the paint layer would support cleaning, which challenges the patina view rather than the older one; viewers preferring cleaned paintings is about modern taste, not about nineteenth-century practice. Trap: Choosing evidence aimed at the patina view, not the older one.

passages.title: The Unfair Persuader
text: Defenders of advertising aimed at children usually make two arguments. Advertising, they say, is a form of speech that informs consumers about products, and parents, who control the household budget, stand between the child and any purchase. Both arguments assume a listener who can recognize persuasion as persuasion. Developmental research suggests that this assumption fails for young children: many children under about eight treat commercials as a kind of entertainment or as neutral information, not as messages designed by someone who wants their money.

The case against child-directed advertising is often made on grounds of harm, by linking advertisements to sugary diets or to materialism. Those links are real but contested, and I think they are not the heart of the matter. The deeper wrong lies in an asymmetry. A persuasive message aimed at a person who cannot identify its purpose is closer to manipulation than to argument, because the listener cannot weigh the message against the motive behind it. Even if a child's newfound craving for a cereal led to no harm at all, the exchange would be defective in the way a swindle is defective even when the victim happens to lose nothing.

The parental-gatekeeper defense fares no better. The industry's own term for one of its strategies, “pester power,” reveals the plan: rather than persuading the parent, the advertiser recruits the child as an advocate inside the home. A defense that names parents as the filter cannot easily survive a marketing practice designed to go around them.

I concede that the line is blurry. Older children and teenagers recognize the intent of advertising and yet remain susceptible to it. Recognition, then, is necessary for fair persuasion but not sufficient. For adolescents, the case for restriction must lean on harm-based arguments, which I regard as relevant but less decisive. Yet newer formats complicate even this concession. Sponsored unboxing videos and branded games erase the boundary between content and commercial on which older children depend to recognize a sales pitch. Such formats, I suggest, return older children to the protected class from which their maturity had seemed to remove them.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses the author's central thesis?
o: Advertising to children is wrong mainly because it reliably causes unhealthy eating.
Not quite. Paragraph 2 says the harm argument is not the heart of the matter.
Advertising to young children is wrong chiefly because it targets people who cannot recognize its intent.
Correct: The author says the deeper wrong is aiming persuasion at people who cannot identify its purpose.
Parents should be held fully responsible for whatever advertisements their children watch on television or online.
Not quite. Paragraph 3 rejects the parental-gatekeeper defense.
All advertising directed at people under eighteen should be banned on equal grounds.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 treats teenagers differently, with weaker grounds.
qs.x: Correct: This asks for the central thesis. Paragraph 2 says the harm arguments are not "the heart of the matter" and that "The deeper wrong lies in an asymmetry": a persuasive message aimed at a person "who cannot identify its purpose" is closer to manipulation than argument. So advertising to young children is wrong chiefly because it targets people who cannot recognize its intent. Why the others are wrong: causing unhealthy eating is the harm argument the author calls real but contested and not central; making parents fully responsible is rejected in paragraph 3; banning everything under eighteen contradicts paragraph 4, where harm arguments for adolescents are "less decisive." Trap: Picking the most common argument against advertising instead of the author's own.

qs.q: The author mentions the industry term “pester power” primarily in order to:
o: show that children are more persuasive than adults realize.
Not quite. The point isn't about how persuasive children are.
argue that advertisers have become more honest about their methods.
Not quite. The term shows a plan to go around parents, not honesty.
suggest that parents are to blame for giving in to their children.
Not quite. The author doesn't blame parents; the practice is designed to go around them.
undermine the claim that parents serve as an effective filter between child and advertiser.
Correct: Pester power shows advertisers recruit the child to get past the parent, so parents are not an effective filter.
qs.x: Correct: The question asks why the author mentions "pester power." Paragraph 3 says the term "reveals the plan: rather than persuading the parent, the advertiser recruits the child as an advocate inside the home." It follows that "A defense that names parents as the filter cannot easily survive." So the term undermines the claim that parents are an effective filter. Why the others are wrong: children being more persuasive than adults realize is not the point; advertisers becoming more honest isn't argued, since this is a strategy to go around parents; blaming parents for giving in is never said. Trap: Reading the phrase's surface meaning instead of its role in the argument.

qs.q: The comparison to a swindle in paragraph 2 serves to illustrate that:
o: a persuasive exchange can wrong someone without harm.
Correct: Like a swindle where the victim loses nothing, an exchange can be defective without harm.
children who see advertisements typically lose money or possessions as a result.
Not quite. The comparison is to a swindle where the victim loses nothing.
advertisers knowingly commit crimes that should be prosecuted.
Not quite. The author doesn't say advertisers commit crimes.
harm-based arguments are the strongest case against advertising.
Not quite. The paragraph calls harm arguments not the heart of the matter.
qs.x: Correct: This asks what the swindle comparison illustrates. Paragraph 2 says that even if a craving "led to no harm at all, the exchange would be defective in the way a swindle is defective even when the victim happens to lose nothing." So a persuasive exchange can wrong someone without causing harm. Why the others are wrong: children typically losing money contradicts "lose nothing"; advertisers committing prosecutable crimes isn't claimed; harm-based arguments being strongest is the opposite of the paragraph. Trap: Taking a comparison to a crime literally.

qs.q: Which new finding would most weaken the author's argument regarding young children?
o: Children exposed to more food advertising consume slightly more sugar.
Not quite. The author already treats harm links as not central.
Teenagers who recognize advertising intent still buy advertised products about as often as younger children do.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says older children recognize intent and yet remain susceptible, which fits.
Most children as young as four can reliably explain that commercials try to make people buy things.
Correct: If young children can explain that commercials aim to sell, the premise that they can't recognize intent fails.
Parents report frequent arguments with their children over toys the children saw advertised on television.
Not quite. Arguments over toys fit the pester power strategy.
qs.x: Correct: This asks which finding would most weaken the argument about young children. Paragraph 1 says many children under about eight don't recognize persuasion as persuasion, and the whole argument rests on that. If most four-year-olds could reliably explain that commercials try to make people buy things, the premise would fail. Why the others are wrong: slightly more sugar consumption is a harm finding, which the author says is not central; teenagers buying as often as younger children fits paragraph 4's point that recognition isn't sufficient; arguments over toys fit the pester power point. Trap: Choosing a harm finding when the argument rests on recognition.

qs.q: Based on the passage, the author would most likely regard an undisclosed video in which a popular host plays with toys supplied by their maker as:
o: acceptable for older children, since they understand advertising intent.
Not quite. Older children rely on spotting the boundary, which this video hides.
harmless as long as no purchase follows from viewing it.
Not quite. The author's concern is hidden intent, not only purchases.
less troubling than a standard commercial, because it does not directly ask any viewer to make a purchase.
Not quite. The lack of a direct ask is what hides the persuasion.
especially objectionable, because it hides the persuasive intent that older children rely on detecting.
Correct: Hiding the persuasive intent takes away what older children rely on to recognize a sales pitch.
qs.x: Correct: This applies paragraph 4. Sponsored unboxing videos and branded games "erase the boundary between content and commercial on which older children depend to recognize a sales pitch." An undisclosed video of a host playing with a maker's toys hides the persuasive intent, so the author would find it especially objectionable. Why the others are wrong: acceptable for older children because they understand advertising ignores that the format hides the pitch; harmless unless a purchase follows is the harm view the author calls less decisive; less troubling because it doesn't ask for a purchase misses that hidden persuasion is the problem. Trap: Assuming a pitch must be explicit to count.

qs.q: Which best describes the author's attitude toward harm-based arguments against child-directed advertising?
o: They are irrelevant and should be abandoned by critics of advertising.
Not quite. The author calls them relevant.
They matter but are less decisive than unrecognized intent.
Correct: The author calls them relevant but less decisive than the manipulation argument.
They are conclusive for young children but irrelevant for adolescents.
Not quite. Paragraph 4 says adolescents' case must lean on harm arguments.
They are stronger than the manipulation argument once complete data on children's health are available.
Not quite. The author never says more data would make them stronger.
qs.x: Correct: This asks the author's attitude toward harm-based arguments. Paragraph 2 calls the harm links "real but contested" and "not the heart of the matter"; paragraph 4 calls them "relevant but less decisive." So they matter but are less decisive than unrecognized intent. Why the others are wrong: irrelevant and to be abandoned contradicts "relevant"; conclusive for young children but irrelevant for adolescents is the reverse of paragraph 4; stronger once complete health data are available isn't said. Trap: Choosing an extreme for or against.
